Confidence Is Not a Promise: A Reference Audit of Typed Decision Models

 Pedro Carvalho Brom Affiliation: Department of Mathematics Affiliation: Federal Institute of Brasília Affiliation: Brasília, Brazil Email: pedro.brom@ifb.edu.br
Abstract

Typed decision models return a probability distribution over options supplied by the caller, and software tends to act on that number as if it were a guarantee. We measure what it licenses, comparing the open-weight Laya, in five checkpoints, with Jev 1.13, available only through an API. A probability licenses a statement about groups of decisions, not about one decision, and a gate that promises an accuracy among the cases it decides alone keeps that promise only with a lower bound checked on data like its traffic. Across 190 exchangeable evaluations, a threshold chosen by point estimate breaks the promise in 147, Learn then Test keeps it in all of them, and a Beta lower-bound rule decides more items on average than Learn then Test in 128 and fewer in none, without its guarantee. Calibrated in English, Jev keeps a promise of 95% in 8 of 51 locales. Ordinary typing noise breaks a promise calibrated on clean text, and, in exploratory runs, training with noise raises the noisy accuracy with no loss on clean text. In four further domains, a fine-tuned Laya needs from 250 to 8,000 labels to be non-inferior to Jev, and does not get there on LIAR2. Under drift, the preregistered claim for a Bayesian retraining loop is not supported: the loop avoids needless retraining where the change does not degrade the model, at a cost equivalent to recalibration alone, and re-qualifying the threshold in every window keeps the promise more often where it does. On the monthly series of M3, neither decider predicts the direction of the next value better than a constant answer. Confidence separates right from wrong answers with an AUROC from 0.80 to 0.96, but it does not select faithful explanations, and exact coalition games of single decisions show what an explanation can still say through an API that rounds to two decimals. We release the frozen answers with a datasheet, a promise check and the code.

   

A Preprint

Keywords typed decision models ⋅\cdot calibration ⋅\cdot selective classification ⋅\cdot explanation fidelity ⋅\cdot auditing

1 Introduction

Much of the decision logic in software consists of choices among options that change from call to call and arrive written in natural language: which department should handle a message, whether a contract contains a termination clause, how irritated a customer is. A classifier whose output layer has one column per class cannot serve these choices, because the number and the meaning of the classes are fixed in its weights. A large language model can serve them by generating an answer that code then parses, at the cost of one forward pass per generated token and of a probability for each option that has to be reconstructed from token probabilities.

A recent class of models, which its first vendor calls System One [TypeSafe, 2026], takes a third route. A typed decision model receives a state, a question and a set of options described in text, and returns a probability distribution over those options in a single pass. Laya [NandhaKishorM, 2026], with open weights, and Jev, available only through an API [TypeSafe, 2026], share this interface. The output is directly usable by code: a decision, a probability and a confidence. That convenience raises the question this paper studies. When such a model returns “billing, 0.97”, what does the number license, and what does it not?

A talk from a security perspective, used here as an example, phrases the question as two statements [IBM Technology, 2026]: confidence is not proof, and a probability is not an explanation. We turn both statements into measurements. The contributions are the following.

  1. 1.

    A formal account of the measures that bear on trusting a typed decider, with their calibration, the error types of the gate, its Bayes threshold and its multi-objective formulation, and the number of labels a Beta gate needs before it can promise anything, which is the Bayesian success-run bound (Section 4).

  2. 2.

    A paired comparison of five Laya checkpoints and Jev 1.13 on 2,000 MASSIVE utterances per language in Portuguese and English, with fine-tuning and its measured training cost, a test of the vendor’s statement about probability one, and a measurement of the relation between a decision’s probability and the fidelity of its explanation (Sections 5 and 6).

  3. 3.

    A replication, for typed deciders, of the gap between point-estimate and certified thresholds, measured against a plug-in population with Monte Carlo and item-level uncertainty separated, and an evaluation of the Beta lower-bound gate [Barkan et al., 2023]: its exact relation to Learn then Test, a proposition on when its ascending scan inherits the guarantee of Learn then Test and why it fails otherwise, the coverage that scan buys and the risk it costs, and an ablation over 60 configurations that attributes the effect to the bound rather than to the prior (Sections 6.3 and 6.4).

  4. 4.

    An exact coalition-game analysis of single decisions that states, for each kind of explanation, when it helps a caller decide whether a decision could be overturned by a small change to the input. Words and pairs suffice for short inputs, interaction indices detect redundant evidence even through an API that rounds, no tested method gives calibrated intervals for the effect of a word under that rounding, confidence does not select faithful explanations, a contrastive explanation holds only for the options it was computed on, and an additive head is not a useful route to exactness at a cost of about 30 points of accuracy (Section 11).

  5. 5.

    A measurement of natural noise and adversarial typos, showing that a gate calibrated on clean text breaks its promise on noisy text, that a probability of 0.9999 does not protect a decision from a single typo, and that training with noise raises the noisy accuracy with no loss on clean text (Section 7).

  6. 6.

    A measurement of how far a promise travels: across 52 locales, where a gate calibrated on Jev in English keeps a promise of 95% in 8 of 51 locales, and across four further domains, where the labels a fine-tuned Laya needs to be non-inferior to Jev range from 250 to 8,000 and its accuracy on LIAR2 is bounded by what the input carries (Sections 8 and 9).

  7. 7.

    A preregistered drift experiment that states when each repair is useful: a Bayesian retraining loop where the change does not degrade the model, re-qualifying the threshold in every window where it does, forgetting faster in per-bin gates, which a dynamic-model gate with its conditions (Proposition 7) reproduces without adding to it, and, on the monthly series of M3, a model of the series rather than a typed decider (Sections 10, 10.4 and 10.5).

  8. 8.

    A reference package for auditing typed deciders: the frozen answers of both deciders with a datasheet, a check of a selective-accuracy promise across populations, and the code that produces every number of the article.

  9. 9.

    A validation protocol that separates what a vendor states, what code does, what was measured and what is not published, and maps seven operational controls to measurements (Section 12).

Table 1 lists each claim of the abstract with its status under the rule of Section 4.7, the evidence behind it and the section that reports it, so that a reader can cite a claim with its strength.

Section 2 places these contributions among recent independent evaluations of typed deciders and the literature on selective prediction with guarantees, which already contains the frequentist counterpart of the rule studied here.

2 Related work

Typed decision models under evaluation.

Since the first typed deciders became available in 2026, an independent literature has asked three questions about them. The first is whether their probabilities are calibrated. Jev 1.13 is found well calibrated and useful for selective prediction on 37 datasets [Deußer et al., 2026], but wording-sensitive and systematically underconfident on a synthetic benchmark built from policy-labelled generators, to the point that under asymmetric costs its probabilities can be worse than its top answer [Sharma et al., 2026]. The Laya typed-decisions checkpoint is uniformly underconfident and repaired by one temperature, while a frozen gate misses its error target [Nandakishore, 2026]. Calibration measured on familiar tasks does not signal missing knowledge [Shankaranarayana et al., 2026], and on Indonesian regional languages Jev’s calibration error does not grow while its ranking of its own errors degrades [Fadli et al., 2026]. The second question is how they compare with other deciders: Laya and Jev in pairs at eleven decision points of agent harnesses, including a MASSIVE subset of ten items per locale [Li, 2026], eight decision checkpoints against trained classifiers and generative models, with the fraction of intent decisions left to Jev under a guaranteed 5% risk [Rafe and Das, 2026], and Jev against a frontier LLM on claim verification at a 187-fold cost difference [Do Rosario and Atef, 2026]. The third is whether a decision holds together. Jev and the English Laya checkpoint disagree with themselves when a decision is decomposed [Joy, 2026], and calibration with allow, block and defer policies has been evaluated for prompt-injection detection under distribution shift [Lan et al., 2026]. An audit of the first 28 papers derives a 14-item evaluation checklist [Tang and Zheng, 2026]. Relative to this literature, the present study measures what a promise of accuracy among accepted decisions is worth across the conditions a deployment meets, from the calibration sample to noise, 52 languages, five domains and drift, with one open and one closed decider, fine-tuning and its cost, the explanation of single decisions and a literal test of the vendor’s statement about probability one, and it releases the answers it measured.

Selective prediction with a promise.

Abstaining when confidence is low goes back to Chow’s rule [Chow, 1970], and selective classification makes the trade between coverage and risk explicit [El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017]. Selection with guaranteed risk [Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017] bounds the selective risk by a binomial tail with a union bound over a binary search. The violation rate over calibration draws that a gate controls is the training-conditional, or PAC, guarantee of conformal prediction [Vovk, 2012; Park et al., 2020]. Risk-controlling prediction sets [Bates et al., 2021] and Learn then Test [Angelopoulos et al., 2025] turn the choice of a threshold into multiple testing with finite-sample guarantees, conformal risk control extends the idea to monotone losses [Angelopoulos et al., 2024], selection by conformal pp-values controls the false discovery rate among selected items [Jin and Candès, 2023], and linear expectation constraints control the error probability conditional on selection [Wang et al., 2025]. On the Bayesian side, conformal prediction has been recast as Bayesian quadrature [Snell and Griffiths, 2025]. Pareto testing combines the multi-objective search with these guarantees [Laufer-Goldshtein et al., 2022]. The cost of ignoring the guarantee has been measured repeatedly: naive thresholds exceed their budget in about half of the settings for binary System One decisions [Messoudi and Mansar, 2026] and in 49% to 73% of trials for signal detectors [Zhou and Wang, 2026], and Basu [2026] ablate nine families of bounds, including the Clopper–Pearson bound in the fixed-sequence procedure of Learn then Test, on MASSIVE among other datasets. The Clopper–Pearson lower bound is the equal-tailed bound of an improper Beta⁡(0,1)\mathrm{Beta}(0,1) posterior [Hofer and Held, 2022; Brown et al., 2001], which makes the relation between the Bayesian rule studied here and Learn then Test exact rather than approximate (Section 6.4). The contribution here is not a new bound. It is a replication of the gap between point-estimate and certified thresholds for typed deciders, measured against a plug-in population with its uncertainty separated, and an evaluation of the Bayesian lower-bound rule with a uniform prior, described by Barkan et al. [2023] for classification thresholds, against Learn then Test and the point estimate: what it buys, what it costs, and where its behaviour comes from. Threshold-based auto-labelling picks the lowest threshold whose estimated error stays below a target with a frequentist bound [Vishwakarma et al., 2023], and approximate selection with a precision target does the same with a correction for multiplicity [Kang et al., 2020]. Beta posteriors for model evaluation with few labels are advocated by Bowyer et al. [2025] and Benavoli et al. [2017], and the optimism of a threshold selected on the same data is an instance of the selection bias documented by Cawley and Talbot [2010] and Tibshirani and Tibshirani [2009].

Calibration.

Temperature scaling [Guo et al., 2017] remains the standard recalibration for neural classifiers and pre-trained transformers [Desai and Durrett, 2020; Minderer et al., 2021]. Top-label calibration is the notion that a thresholded decision needs [Gupta and Ramdas, 2022], the binned ECE can underestimate the calibration error of a continuous predictor [Kumar et al., 2019], and a single temperature is known to fail unevenly across the confidence range and under shift [Joy et al., 2023; Ovadia et al., 2019]. The tail failure reported below is an instance of the last point for a typed decider, measured where an extreme cost ratio places the threshold.

Explanation fidelity.

Fidelity is the degree to which an explanation reflects the reasoning of the model [Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020]. Deletion and comprehensiveness metrics [Samek et al., 2017; Petsiuk et al., 2018; DeYoung et al., 2020] remove what the explanation points to, and sanity checks and retraining benchmarks warn that such measures can reward explanations unrelated to the model [Adebayo et al., 2018; Hooker et al., 2019]. For decision models, Ahmed [2026] use leave-one-symptom-out perturbations, and Tropeano et al. [2026] report that faithfulness and calibration move independently under pruning. We are not aware of a measurement of the relation between a typed decider’s probability and the fidelity of its explanation item by item. Attributions that average over coalitions have uncertainty-aware estimators [Slack et al., 2020; Covert and Lee, 2020], interactions between words can be detected hierarchically [Chen et al., 2020], and planted shortcuts give a ground truth for faithfulness in text [Bastings et al., 2021]. Their behaviour when the decider returns rounded probabilities, as a closed API does, has not been measured to our knowledge.

3 Typed decision models

3.1 Definition

Let ss be a state (text, a JSON object or a list of messages), qq an instruction and 𝒪=(o1,…,ok)\mathcal{O}=(o_{1},\dots,o_{k}) a list of options, each with a textual description. A typed decision model is a map

fθ:(s,q,𝒪)⟼𝐩∈Δk−1,Δk−1={𝐩∈ℝk:pj≥0,∑j=1kpj=1},f_{\theta}:(s,q,\mathcal{O})\longmapsto\mathbf{p}\in\Delta^{k-1},\qquad\Delta^{k-1}=\Big\{\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}:p_{j}\geq 0,\ \textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{k}p_{j}=1\Big\}, (1)

where kk is chosen by the caller. Since no parameter may depend on kk, the score of each option is produced by a function shared across options,

zj=gθ​(s,q,oj∣𝒪),pj=exp⁡(zj/T)∑l=1kexp⁡(zl/T),z_{j}=g_{\theta}(s,q,o_{j}\mid\mathcal{O}),\qquad p_{j}=\frac{\exp(z_{j}/T)}{\sum_{l=1}^{k}\exp(z_{l}/T)}, (2)

with temperature T>0T>0. The conditioning on 𝒪\mathcal{O} allows each option to be scored in the light of the others. Three question types are exposed: choice returns 𝐩\mathbf{p} and its mode. noul is the case k=2k=2 and returns pyesp_{\text{yes}}. score takes LL ordered levels and returns the expected level s^=∑i=0L−1i​pi\hat{s}=\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}i\,p_{i}, not the most probable one.

3.2 Two ways of returning a probability

An autoregressive language model factorises the probability of a token sequence as ∏tpθ​(xt∣x<t)\prod_{t}p_{\theta}(x_{t}\mid x_{<t}). Used as a decider, the probability of an option written with tokens (w1,…,wm)(w_{1},\dots,w_{m}) is ∏ipθ​(wi∣prompt,w<i)\prod_{i}p_{\theta}(w_{i}\mid\text{prompt},w_{<i}), and the sum of these over 𝒪\mathcal{O} is at most one, the remainder being mass on any other text. A typed decider returns a distribution on 𝒪\mathcal{O} itself, at a cost of one pass per question. Neither pre-training by likelihood of the next token nor preference optimisation [Ouyang et al., 2022] requires the stated probability of an answer to match its frequency of being right, and language models are known to be imperfectly calibrated about their own answers [Kadavath et al., 2022]. The typed deciders studied here state calibration as a training goal: Jev through a reinforcement-learning stage the vendor calls RLCD [TypeSafe, 2026], and Laya through a reward built from strictly proper scoring rules (logarithmic, spherical and ranked probability score) optimised by policy gradient together with cross-entropy, according to its code [NandhaKishorM, 2026].

3.3 The two models

Laya places one [MASK] token before each option in the input sequence [CLS]τ(t,q)[SEP][MASK]τ(o1)⋯[MASK]τ(ok)[SEP]τ(s)[SEP][\texttt{CLS}]\ \tau(t,q)\ [\texttt{SEP}]\ [\texttt{MASK}]\,\tau(o_{1})\cdots[\texttt{MASK}]\,\tau(o_{k})\ [\texttt{SEP}]\ \tau(s)\ [\texttt{SEP}], where τ\tau is the tokenizer and tt the question type. A bidirectional encoder [Devlin et al., 2019; Vaswani et al., 2017] produces 𝐇∈ℝn×d\mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, an embedding of the question type is added, a two-layer Transformer head mixes the positions, and a single MLP maps the vector at each anchor to the score zjz_{j}. The multilingual checkpoint uses mmBERT-base [Marone et al., 2025] with 322 million parameters and a budget of 1,024 tokens, beyond which the state is truncated without warning. The English checkpoint and the typed-decisions checkpoint, fine-tuned by the developer of Laya on the developer’s own benchmark, use ModernBERT-large [Warner et al., 2025]. Jev 1.13 is documented only through its interface, a context of 64 thousand tokens per request, English as primary training language, and its training family [TypeSafe, 2026]. Its architecture, size, data and reward are not published, and nothing about its internals is assumed here.

4 Measures and their calibration

Throughout, a decider answers nn items. Item ii has gold option yiy_{i}, probabilities 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i}, decision y^i=arg​maxj⁡pij\hat{y}_{i}=\argmax_{j}p_{ij} and correctness indicator ai=𝟏[y^i=yi]a_{i}=\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i}].

4.1 Three confidences

Three functions of 𝐩\mathbf{p} are reported as confidence by the systems studied:

cmax=maxjpj,cH=1−H⁡(𝐩)log⁡k,H(𝐩)=−∑jpjlogpj,cJ=k​cmax−1k−1.c_{\max}=\max_{j}p_{j},\qquad c_{H}=1-\frac{H(\mathbf{p})}{\log k},\ \ H(\mathbf{p})=-\sum_{j}p_{j}\log p_{j},\qquad c_{\text{J}}=\frac{k\,c_{\max}-1}{k-1}. (3)

Laya returns cmaxc_{\max} as answer_confidence and cHc_{H} as confidence, and Jev returns cJc_{\text{J}} [TypeSafe, 2026].

Proposition 1.

For fixed k≥2k\geq 2, cJc_{\text{J}} is a strictly increasing affine function of cmaxc_{\max}. Hence for every threshold τ\tau on cmaxc_{\max} there is a threshold τ′=(k​τ−1)/(k−1)\tau^{\prime}=(k\tau-1)/(k-1) on cJc_{\text{J}} that accepts exactly the same items. For k=2k=2, cHc_{H} is a strictly increasing function of cmaxc_{\max} and thresholds on the two correspond. For k≥3k\geq 3 no such correspondence holds: there are vectors ordered one way by cmaxc_{\max} and the other way by cHc_{H}.

The proof is in Appendix A. Because only cmaxc_{\max} is the quantity that temperature scaling adjusts and that calibration refers to, all gates below are thresholds on cmaxc_{\max}, written CC.

4.2 Calibration

Definition 1 (Top-label calibration).

A decider is calibrated in its top label when ℙ⁡(Y^=Y∣C=c)=c\mathbb{P}(\hat{Y}=Y\mid C=c)=c for almost every c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1].

Calibration is a property of groups of predictions: it states how often the answers given with confidence cc are right, and says nothing about any single answer. Its usual estimator partitions [0,1][0,1] into BB equal bins ℬb\mathcal{B}_{b} and averages the gap between accuracy and confidence [Naeini et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017]:

ECE=∑b=1B|ℬb|n​|a¯​(ℬb)−c¯​(ℬb)|,B=15.\text{ECE}=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{|\mathcal{B}_{b}|}{n}\,\Big|\,\overline{a}(\mathcal{B}_{b})-\overline{c}(\mathcal{B}_{b})\,\Big|,\qquad B=15. (4)

ECE is not a proper score and depends on the binning, and with few items per bin it is biased upwards. We therefore also report two strictly proper scores [Gneiting and Raftery, 2007], the Brier score and the negative log-likelihood,

BS=1n∑i∑j(pi​j−𝟏[yi=j])2,NLL=−1n∑ilogpi,yi.\text{BS}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\sum_{j}\big(p_{ij}-\mathbf{1}[y_{i}=j]\big)^{2},\qquad\text{NLL}=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\log p_{i,y_{i}}. (5)

A scoring rule S⁡(𝐩,y)S(\mathbf{p},y), with positive orientation, is strictly proper when 𝔼y∼𝐪​S​(𝐪,y)>𝔼y∼𝐪​S​(𝐩,y)\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mathbf{q}}S(\mathbf{q},y)>\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mathbf{q}}S(\mathbf{p},y) for all 𝐩≠𝐪\mathbf{p}\neq\mathbf{q}: reporting the true distribution is the unique optimal strategy. This is the sense in which a training objective built from such rules “rewards honest probabilities”. It is a property of the objective, not a guarantee about a trained model on a new distribution, which is why calibration is measured here rather than assumed.

Temperature scaling.

A single inverse temperature β=1/T\beta=1/T applied to log-probabilities 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i} is fitted on held-out data by minimising

ℒ(β)=1n∑i=1n[−βzi,yi+log∑j=1keβ​zi​j]\mathcal{L}(\beta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[-\beta z_{i,y_{i}}+\log\sum_{j=1}^{k}e^{\beta z_{ij}}\Big] (6)

[Guo et al., 2017].

Proposition 2.

ℒ\mathcal{L} is convex on ℝ\mathbb{R}, with ℒ′​(β)=1n​∑i(𝔼𝐩i​(β)​[zi]−zi,yi)\mathcal{L}^{\prime}(\beta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{p}_{i}(\beta)}[z_{i}]-z_{i,y_{i}}) and ℒ′′​(β)=1n​∑iVar𝐩i​(β)​[zi]≥0\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}(\beta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\mathrm{Var}_{\mathbf{p}_{i}(\beta)}[z_{i}]\geq 0, where 𝐩i​(β)=softmax⁡(β​𝐳i)\mathbf{p}_{i}(\beta)=\mathrm{softmax}(\beta\mathbf{z}_{i}). It is strictly convex when some item has non-constant scores. A minimiser need not exist: if every item has zi,yi>maxj≠yi⁡zi​jz_{i,y_{i}}>\max_{j\neq y_{i}}z_{ij}, then ℒ′​(β)<0\mathcal{L}^{\prime}(\beta)<0 for all β\beta and the infimum is approached as β→∞\beta\to\infty.

If some calibration item is wrong, ℒ′​(β)\mathcal{L}^{\prime}(\beta) tends to a positive limit as β→∞\beta\to\infty, so a minimiser exists whenever ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} is negative somewhere, and the strict convexity makes it unique. Temperatures are fitted below by Newton’s method β←β−ℒ′​(β)/ℒ′′​(β)\beta\leftarrow\beta-\mathcal{L}^{\prime}(\beta)/\mathcal{L}^{\prime\prime}(\beta), with the iterate clipped to [0.05,20][0.05,20] as a safeguard. The fitted temperatures reported here lie between 0.40 and 1.77, inside that range. A temperature cannot correct a decider that returns probabilities already rounded, as Jev does: rounded to two decimals, about three quarters of its answers put exactly 1.00 on one option, so z=log⁡pz=\log p is −∞-\infty on the others and no β\beta changes them. Jev is evaluated as returned.

4.3 Confidence as a detector of correct answers

Calibration measures whether the value of confidence is honest. It does not measure whether confidence orders cases well. The second property is measured by the receiver operating characteristic of CC as a score for the event A=1A=1. Accepting the items with C≥τC\geq\tau accepts a fraction TPR⁡(τ)=ℙ⁡(C≥τ∣A=1)\mathrm{TPR}(\tau)=\mathbb{P}(C\geq\tau\mid A=1) of correct answers and a fraction FPR⁡(τ)=ℙ⁡(C≥τ∣A=0)\mathrm{FPR}(\tau)=\mathbb{P}(C\geq\tau\mid A=0) of wrong ones. The area under this curve equals the Mann–Whitney probability

AUROC=ℙ⁡(C+>C−)+12​ℙ​(C+=C−),\text{AUROC}=\mathbb{P}(C^{+}>C^{-})+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{P}(C^{+}=C^{-}), (7)

where C+C^{+} and C−C^{-} are the confidences of an independently drawn correct and wrong answer [Hanley and McNeil, 1982]. Confidence would be proof of correctness only if AUROC were 1.

4.4 Explanation fidelity

A probability states how much the model believes its decision, and an explanation should state why. We test the simplest form of an explanation, a ranking of input words by importance, by removing what it points to [Zeiler and Fergus, 2014; Samek et al., 2017; Petsiuk et al., 2018]. For a state with words w1,…,wmw_{1},\dots,w_{m} and decided option o^\hat{o}, the occlusion importance of word wlw_{l} is Il=po^​(s)−po^​(s∖wl)I_{l}=p_{\hat{o}}(s)-p_{\hat{o}}(s\setminus w_{l}). Removing words cumulatively in decreasing order of IlI_{l} gives the deletion curve

D⁡(x)=min⁡{1,po^​(s∖{w(1),…,w(⌊x​m⌋)})po^​(s)},x∈[0,1],D(x)=\min\Big\{1,\ \frac{p_{\hat{o}}(s\setminus\{w_{(1)},\dots,w_{(\lfloor xm\rfloor)}\})}{p_{\hat{o}}(s)}\Big\},\qquad x\in[0,1], (8)

and its area AUD=∫01D⁡(x)​𝑑x\text{AUD}=\int_{0}^{1}D(x)\,dx, approximated on an 11-point grid. A faithful explanation makes the decision collapse early, giving a small area. The reference is the same curve with words removed in random order. Because the same perturbation defines and evaluates the importance, and because deleting words produces inputs unlike the training data [Hooker et al., 2019], the comparison with the random order is essential and the measure is read as a lower standard than retraining-based benchmarks.

4.5 The selective gate

A gate decides alone when C≥τC\geq\tau and escalates the rest to a person [El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017]. Its coverage and the accuracy among the cases it accepts are

ϕ⁡(τ)=ℙ⁡(C≥τ),θ⁡(τ)=ℙ⁡(A=1∣C≥τ).\phi(\tau)=\mathbb{P}(C\geq\tau),\qquad\theta(\tau)=\mathbb{P}(A=1\mid C\geq\tau). (9)

The slack of a promise.

At a threshold that keeps the promise, the slack is θ⁡(τ)−α\theta(\tau)-\alpha, the accuracy the accepted items can lose before the promise breaks. A change of the input that lowers θ⁡(τ)\theta(\tau) by more than the slack breaks the promise whatever rule chose τ\tau, and Sections 7, 8 and 9 measure such changes. How high θ\theta can be pushed in the first place is bounded by Proposition 6.

Two error types.

Among accepted answers, a wrong one is a type I error: a wrong action executed without anyone seeing it. Among escalated answers, a correct one is a type II error: a person reviews what was already right. Reading the gate as a test of H0H_{0}: “the answer is wrong”, accepting is rejecting H0H_{0}, and a promise θ⁡(τ)≥α\theta(\tau)\geq\alpha bounds the fraction of wrong answers among acceptances, 1−θ⁡(τ)1-\theta(\tau), which is a false discovery rate rather than a type I error rate in the Neyman–Pearson sense. Which error is worse is not a statistical question. It depends on the action the system executes and must be fixed with whoever is accountable for the process.

The F1 of the gate.

With TP\mathrm{TP} the accepted correct answers, FP\mathrm{FP} the accepted wrong ones and FN\mathrm{FN} the escalated correct ones, F1=2​TP/(2​TP+FP+FN)F_{1}=2\mathrm{TP}/(2\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{FN}). It ignores the escalated wrong answers and weighs the two error types almost symmetrically, so maximising it pushes the gate to accept nearly everything.

Reviews per avoided error.

Relative to a reference rule, a rule that escalates Δr\Delta_{r} more items per 1,000 and executes Δe\Delta_{e} fewer wrong actions pays Δr/Δe\Delta_{r}/\Delta_{e} reviews per avoided wrong action. It is the cost ratio Ce/CrC_{e}/C_{r} at which the two rules cost the same, so the stricter rule is worth it exactly when a wrong action costs more than that many reviews.

The Bayes threshold.

Let a wrong automatic action cost CeC_{e} and each escalation cost CrC_{r}, with 0<Cr<Ce0<C_{r}<C_{e}.

Proposition 3.

If the decider is calibrated in its top label, the rule that accepts exactly when C>τ∗=1−Cr/CeC>\tau^{*}=1-C_{r}/C_{e} minimises the expected cost per item among all rules that decide from CC alone.

The proof is a pointwise comparison of two conditional expected costs (Appendix A). The proposition separates two steps that are often merged: calibration, by a proper score, makes the probability honest, and the metric of the problem then chooses the threshold. Fitting a temperature to maximise F1 or minimise cost would distort the probability that the threshold formula needs.

The conditional promise and the point rule.

A gate promises θ⁡(τ)≥α\theta(\tau)\geq\alpha. On a calibration sample, n⁡(τ)n(\tau) items pass the threshold and c⁡(τ)c(\tau) of them are correct. The point rule scans thresholds from the lowest and keeps the first with θ^​(τ)=c⁡(τ)/n⁡(τ)≥α\hat{\theta}(\tau)=c(\tau)/n(\tau)\geq\alpha, requiring n⁡(τ)≥20n(\tau)\geq 20.

Remark 1.

The estimate θ^​(τ)\hat{\theta}(\tau) has standard error θ⁡(1−θ)/n\sqrt{\theta(1-\theta)/n}, which is 0.44 percentage points for θ=0.99\theta=0.99 and n=500n=500. If θ⁡(τ)\theta(\tau) decreases continuously with coverage and θ^\hat{\theta} is approximately normal around it, the point rule stops where the estimate first reaches α\alpha, that is at a threshold whose true conditional accuracy is close to α\alpha, and the promise then holds on new data with probability close to one half. This is a heuristic argument, not a theorem: the scan introduces dependence between thresholds. Section 6.3 measures the rate.

The Beta lower-bound rule.

The rule evaluated here as an alternative replaces the point estimate by a Bayesian lower bound. The same rule, a Beta posterior on precision with a uniform prior, a credibility requirement at a target precision and the qualifying candidate of largest recall, was described by Barkan et al. [2023] for setting the threshold of a classifier, and a frequentist analogue of its minimum-threshold sweep is the threshold estimator of Vishwakarma et al. [2023]. Applied to one threshold, its criterion is the Bayesian binomial reliability-demonstration test with a uniform prior [Wilson and Farrow, 2021]. It is also the gate of the open companion material for Laya, which motivates its evaluation here. The rule treats θ⁡(τ)\theta(\tau) as uncertain given the accepted cases. Under a uniform prior and exchangeable outcomes among accepted items,

θ⁡(τ)|c,n∼Beta⁡(c+1,n−c+1),\theta(\tau)\mid c,n\sim\mathrm{Beta}\big(c+1,\ n-c+1\big), (10)

and the rule keeps the lowest threshold for which the 5% quantile of this posterior is at least α\alpha, with the same minimum of 20 accepted cases. In words: a threshold is accepted only if, with posterior credibility 0.95, the accuracy among the accepted cases exceeds the target. High thresholds leave few accepted cases, which widens the posterior and makes the rule more demanding, and when no threshold qualifies, the gate decides nothing. The statement is Bayesian. It is not a frequentist guarantee, and it inherits a selection effect when qualification is rare: thresholds then qualify mostly on calibration samples that happened to be favourable. The scan matters: in this rule, every candidate threshold is examined and the lowest one that qualifies is kept, wherever it lies in the scan. We call this the ascending scan, and the variant that walks down from the highest threshold and stops at the first one that fails the fixed-sequence scan.

Learn then Test and SGR.

Two frequentist rules serve as references. Learn then Test (LTT) [Angelopoulos et al., 2025] tests, for each candidate threshold τj\tau_{j} with njn_{j} accepted and cjc_{j} correct calibration items, the null hypothesis θ⁡(τj)<α\theta(\tau_{j})<\alpha with the binomial pp-value pj=ℙ⁡(Bin⁡(nj,α)≥cj)p_{j}=\mathbb{P}\big(\mathrm{Bin}(n_{j},\alpha)\geq c_{j}\big), in fixed sequence from the highest threshold, skipping thresholds where even cj=njc_{j}=n_{j} cannot reject (αnj>δ\alpha^{n_{j}}>\delta) and stopping at the first pj>δp_{j}>\delta. With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over the calibration sample, the chosen threshold satisfies θ⁡(τ^)≥α\theta(\hat{\tau})\geq\alpha. Selection with guaranteed risk (SGR) [Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017] searches the mm candidates by bisection and accepts a threshold when the Clopper–Pearson upper bound of its error rate at level δ/⌈log2⁡m⌉\delta/\lceil\log_{2}m\rceil is below 1−α1-\alpha.

Remark 2 (Relation to Learn then Test).

By the identity between the binomial tail and the regularised incomplete beta function, pj≤δp_{j}\leq\delta if and only if α\alpha is at most the δ\delta-quantile of Beta⁡(cj,nj−cj+1)\mathrm{Beta}(c_{j},\,n_{j}-c_{j}+1), the Clopper–Pearson lower bound, which is the equal-tailed bound of the improper prior Beta⁡(0,1)\mathrm{Beta}(0,1) [Brown et al., 2001; Hofer and Held, 2022]. The Beta rule of eq. 10 replaces this prior by the uniform Beta⁡(1,1)\mathrm{Beta}(1,1), one pseudo-success, and Learn then Test is recovered exactly by the Beta rule with prior Beta⁡(0,1)\mathrm{Beta}(0,1), q=δq=\delta and the fixed-sequence scan over testable thresholds. The two rules therefore differ in exactly two choices, the prior and the scan, and Section 6.4 measures the price of each.

The ascending scan has been verified on data, not proved, and the two are different statements. The next result states when the scan inherits a guarantee and why it can fail.

Proposition 4 (When the ascending scan inherits a guarantee).

Order the testable candidate thresholds from the highest, τ1>τ2>⋯>τm\tau_{1}>\tau_{2}>\dots>\tau_{m}, and let Qj=1Q_{j}=1 when τj\tau_{j} qualifies under the Beta rule. The ascending scan returns τJA\tau_{J_{A}} with JA=max⁡{j:Qj=1}J_{A}=\max\{j:Q_{j}=1\}, and the fixed-sequence scan returns τJF\tau_{J_{F}} with JF=max⁡{j:Q1=⋯=Qj=1}J_{F}=\max\{j:Q_{1}=\dots=Q_{j}=1\}, each returning no threshold when its set is empty. Let VAV_{A} and VFV_{F} be the events that the threshold returned by each scan breaks the promise, θ⁡(τ)<α\theta(\tau)<\alpha, and D={JA≠JF}D=\{J_{A}\neq J_{F}\} the event that the scans disagree.

  1. (i)

    The scans agree if and only if the qualifying indices form an initial segment {1,…,k}\{1,\dots,k\}, k≥0k\geq 0, that is, no threshold qualifies below one that fails.

  2. (ii)

    VA⊆VF∪DV_{A}\subseteq V_{F}\cup D, hence ℙ⁡(VA)≤ℙ⁡(VF)+ℙ⁡(D)\mathbb{P}(V_{A})\leq\mathbb{P}(V_{F})+\mathbb{P}(D) and ℙ⁡(VA∩Dc)≤ℙ⁡(VF)\mathbb{P}(V_{A}\cap D^{c})\leq\mathbb{P}(V_{F}).

  3. (iii)

    With the prior Beta⁡(0,1)\mathrm{Beta}(0,1) and q=δq=\delta, the fixed-sequence scan is Learn then Test, and ℙ⁡(VA)≤δ+ℙ⁡(D)\mathbb{P}(V_{A})\leq\delta+\mathbb{P}(D) under the exchangeability that Learn then Test assumes.

The proof is in Appendix A. The prefix form of part (i) is the fixed-sequence procedure of multiple testing [Bauer, 1991; Hsu and Berger, 1999], used for thresholds by risk-controlling prediction sets and Learn then Test [Bates et al., 2021; Angelopoulos et al., 2025], and parts (ii) and (iii) are an elementary decomposition by a union bound, close in form to the argument of Angelopoulos [2026], where the risk of an arbitrary calibration algorithm is bounded by that of a valid reference algorithm plus a gap estimated from the calibration data. The event DD is observable on the calibration sample, since both scans can be run on it, so a deployment can tell whether the threshold it uses came from a qualification pattern that the guarantee covers. Its probability is not observable and has to be estimated, for instance by resampling the calibration items, without a finite-sample guarantee. The bound in (ii) concerns the joint event, so agreement of the scans does not by itself bound the conditional probability of a violation by δ\delta. Part (i) also says where the scan can fail: a threshold must fail and a lower one, which accepts every item of the higher one and more, must qualify again. That needs the added items to be right often enough to lift the lower bound back over the target, which happens where the conditional accuracy is flat or not monotone near α\alpha.

Proposition 5 (Labels the rule needs).

Under the uniform prior, a threshold with nn accepted calibration items can qualify at target α\alpha and credibility level 1−q1-q only if n≥⌈ln⁡q/ln⁡α⌉−1n\geq\lceil\ln q/\ln\alpha\rceil-1.

This is the Bayesian success-run bound. With no failure among nn items the posterior is Beta⁡(n+1,1)\mathrm{Beta}(n+1,1), a computation that goes back to Price’s appendix to the essay of Bayes [1763] and is reviewed by Luko [1997], and its frequentist version with the Beta⁡(0,1)\mathrm{Beta}(0,1) prior is the success-run formula of reliability demonstration and the rule of three [Hanley and Lippman-Hand, 1983]. For q=0.05q=0.05 the bound is 58 accepted items at α=0.95\alpha=0.95, 298 at 0.990.99 and 597 at 0.9950.995, which makes the minimum of 20 accepted cases of the rule inactive at these targets. The proof is in Appendix A.

What no rule can promise.

Every rule above chooses a threshold, and so chooses which items to accept. None of them changes what can be known about an item from its input. Let XX be the input, YY the correct option, ηy​(x)=ℙ⁡(Y=y∣X=x)\eta_{y}(x)=\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid X=x), and m⁡(x)=maxy⁡ηy​(x)m(x)=\max_{y}\eta_{y}(x) the largest probability that any option has given the input.

Proposition 6 (The ceiling of a promise).
  1. (i)

    For every decision function dd and every acceptance set SS with ℙ⁡(X∈S)>0\mathbb{P}(X\in S)>0, ℙ⁡(d⁡(X)=Y∣X∈S)≤𝔼⁡[m⁡(X)∣X∈S]\mathbb{P}\big(d(X)=Y\mid X\in S\big)\leq\mathbb{E}\big[m(X)\mid X\in S\big].

  2. (ii)

    If ℙ⁡(m⁡(X)≥t)=c>0\mathbb{P}(m(X)\geq t)=c>0, then among all decision functions and acceptance sets with ℙ⁡(X∈S)=c\mathbb{P}(X\in S)=c, the accuracy among accepted items is largest for d∗​(x)=arg​maxy⁡ηy​(x)d^{*}(x)=\argmax_{y}\eta_{y}(x) and S∗={x:m⁡(x)≥t}S^{*}=\{x:m(x)\geq t\}, where it equals Θ∗​(c)=𝔼⁡[m⁡(X)∣m⁡(X)≥t]\Theta^{*}(c)=\mathbb{E}[m(X)\mid m(X)\geq t], and Θ∗\Theta^{*} does not increase with cc.

  3. (iii)

    A promise θ≥α\theta\geq\alpha can therefore be kept at coverage cc only if α≤Θ∗​(c)\alpha\leq\Theta^{*}(c), and at any positive coverage only if α\alpha does not exceed the essential supremum of m⁡(X)m(X).

  4. (iv)

    Observing a further variable WW does not lower the ceiling, ΘX,W∗​(c)≥ΘX∗​(c)\Theta^{*}_{X,W}(c)\geq\Theta^{*}_{X}(c) at every coverage where both are defined, and merging options into coarser ones does not lower mm.

Part (ii) is Chow’s reject rule [Chow, 1970] read as a ceiling: the best selective decider ranks items by mm. The point rule, the Beta rule, Learn then Test and temperature scaling act on the order of a decider’s confidence CC, so the sets they accept have the form {C≥τ}\{C\geq\tau\}, and part (i) bounds their accuracy whatever the rule. A decider reaches Θ∗\Theta^{*} only where its decisions and its order agree with d∗d^{*} and mm, which is what more labels, a better model or a combination of deciders can improve. Only part (iv) raises the ceiling itself, by putting more information in the state or by asking a coarser question. Its first half is the conditional Jensen inequality applied to the convex map v↦maxy⁡vyv\mapsto\max_{y}v_{y} of the posterior, the same argument by which more informative observations never lower the expected value of the best decision [Blackwell, 1953; DeGroot, 1962]. The ceiling of a promise is that general fact read for the accuracy among accepted items. The proof is in Appendix A, and the finite case of (i) and the two inequalities behind (iv) are checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib (proofs/SelectiveCeiling.lean in the repository).

4.6 Multi-objective formulation

The gate trades coverage against risk, and a deployment usually adds constraints by group. Let R⁡(τ)=1−θ⁡(τ)R(\tau)=1-\theta(\tau) be the selective risk.

Pareto set and costs.

Because coverage ϕ\phi falls with τ\tau while RR need not be monotone, only the lower envelope of the risk–coverage curve is Pareto-optimal. Weighting wrong automatic actions against escalations, Jw​(τ)=w​ℙ​(A=0,C≥τ)+(1−w)​ℙ​(C<τ)J_{w}(\tau)=w\,\mathbb{P}(A=0,\,C\geq\tau)+(1-w)\,\mathbb{P}(C<\tau), is the cost model of Proposition 3 with Ce/Cr=w/(1−w)C_{e}/C_{r}=w/(1-w), so each weight w>1/2w>1/2 selects the Bayes threshold τ∗=1−(1−w)/w\tau^{*}=1-(1-w)/w under calibration.

Constrained form.

The promise of the gate is the constrained problem

maxτ⁡ϕ⁡(τ)subject toR⁡(τ)≤1−α,\max_{\tau}\ \phi(\tau)\quad\text{subject to}\quad R(\tau)\leq 1-\alpha, (11)

estimated on a calibration sample. The point and Beta rules are two estimators of its solution, and the Beta rule replaces the constraint by ℙ⁡(R⁡(τ)>1−α∣data)≤0.05\mathbb{P}(R(\tau)>1-\alpha\mid\text{data})\leq 0.05.

Thresholds by class.

When the cost of a wrong action depends on the option, a vector of thresholds (τ1,…,τK)(\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{K}), one per decided label, solves eq. 11 or minimises JwJ_{w} separately on the items decided as each label, at the price of fewer calibration items per threshold.

Multicalibration.

A single temperature calibrates on average. For a collection 𝒢\mathcal{G} of groups (here, MASSIVE scenarios) and confidence bins ℬb\mathcal{B}_{b}, multicalibration asks that

|𝔼[A−C∣X∈G,C∈ℬb]|≤κfor all G∈𝒢 and all b\big|\,\mathbb{E}[A-C\mid X\in G,\ C\in\mathcal{B}_{b}]\,\big|\leq\kappa\qquad\text{for all }G\in\mathcal{G}\text{ and all }b (12)

with enough mass in each cell [Hébert-Johnson et al., 2018]. A low global ECE can hide groups that violate eq. 12, which Section 6.2 measures.

4.7 Comparing two methods: superiority, non-inferiority, equivalence and efficiency

Many of the comparisons below ask whether one method is better than another, and a method that is no worse at a lower cost is already a gain. Saying so requires stating what “no worse” means and how it is tested, because the usual reading of a confidence interval that contains zero, as evidence that two methods are alike, is not valid [Walker and Nowacki, 2011]. We use the following definitions throughout. Accuracy comparisons use a margin of 2 points, the margin preregistered for the additive head of Section 11 (criterion G4) and kept for every later comparison of accuracy. It is set by the resolution of the measurement, not by a cost: on 2,000 items an accuracy near 0.95 has a 95% interval of about one point on each side, so a margin of 2 points is the smallest that a paired comparison can show. A caller for whom a wrong action costs much more than a review should use a smaller margin, which the analysis scripts take as a parameter.

Let YAY_{A} and YBY_{B} be an outcome of methods AA and BB for which larger is worse, such as a violation rate, the share of windows below the promise or an error rate, observed in pairs over independent units (calibration draws, streams or items), and let Δ=𝔼⁡[YA−YB]\Delta=\mathbb{E}[Y_{A}-Y_{B}]. A margin ε>0\varepsilon>0 is the largest difference that does not matter in practice. It is fixed before the data are seen, from the smallest difference of practical interest or from a tolerance already stated [Lakens et al., 2018], as the regulatory practice for non-inferiority trials also requires [U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2016].

  • •

    Superiority of AA: the hypothesis H0:Δ≥0H_{0}:\Delta\geq 0 is rejected in favour of Δ<0\Delta<0. It is claimed when the upper limit of the two-sided 95% interval of Δ\Delta is below zero.

  • •

    Non-inferiority of AA to BB: AA may be worse than BB, but by less than the margin. The hypothesis H0:Δ≥εH_{0}:\Delta\geq\varepsilon is rejected in favour of Δ<ε\Delta<\varepsilon by a one-sided test at level 0.025, which is the same as requiring the upper limit of the two-sided 95% interval to lie below ε\varepsilon.

  • •

    Equivalence: H0:|Δ|≥εH_{0}:|\Delta|\geq\varepsilon is rejected in favour of |Δ|<ε|\Delta|<\varepsilon by two one-sided tests at level 0.05 each [Schuirmann, 1987], which is the same as requiring the 90% interval to lie inside (−ε,ε)(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon).

  • •

    No difference detected: an interval that contains zero and meets none of the three conditions. It is reported as such and is never read as equivalence.

A method has an efficiency gain over another when its outcome is non-inferior and it uses less of at least one resource (reviews, retrains, GPU time, model passes) with the upper limit of the paired 95% interval of the difference below zero. The gain is clean when no other resource and no error rate is larger with an interval above zero, and a trade-off otherwise, where one resource is saved by spending another.

The intervals are paired tt intervals over independent units, checked by a bootstrap of the same units where reported. For the gate against the plug-in population, the Monte Carlo error of the calibration draws ignores the sampling of the 2,000 items, so the standard deviation of a difference is taken from 200 bootstrap populations, which includes the item part. Proportions measured on the same items are compared by the exact McNemar test. Comparisons fixed in a preregistration are confirmatory. The others are labelled exploratory, their number is stated, and no correction for multiplicity is applied, so an isolated exploratory result is a lead for further work, not a finding.

5 Experimental setup

Data.

MASSIVE 1.1 [FitzGerald et al., 2023], test split, in pt-PT and en-US. The test split is shuffled with Python’s random generator and seed 13 and its first 2,000 utterances are kept, and each becomes a choice question with five options: the gold intent and four distractors drawn from the other test intents by the same generator, shuffled with the gold intent (scripts/itens_massive.py rebuilds the items from the MASSIVE release). The two languages share the same intents and options item by item, which allows paired comparisons across languages. The instruction is “What is the user asking for in utterance?” and each option is described by its intent name with underscores replaced by spaces. Licence CC BY 4.0.

Systems.

Jev 1.13, answers collected through the API on 2026-09-26 and frozen. Laya at code commit 4066d5d and weights revision 55cf4c4: the multilingual, English and typed-decisions checkpoints without fine-tuning, and, in Portuguese only, the multilingual and typed-decisions checkpoints fine-tuned on the 11,274 MASSIVE pt-PT training utterances that remain after removing 240 exact duplicates of test utterances (three epochs, batch 32, AdamW with learning rates 2.5×10−52.5\times 10^{-5} for the encoder and 10−410^{-4} for the head, recipe in the companion lesson repository). Laya inference ran on CPU in bfloat16 autocast, batches of eight sorted by length. Table 2 fixes the names used in the text and the tables.

Protocol.

Items 0 to 999 calibrate: Laya temperatures are fitted by Newton’s method (Proposition 2) and gate thresholds are chosen there. Items 1,000 to 1,999 report. The gate is also evaluated over 1,000 random calibration/report splits, refitting the Laya temperature on each calibration half. Intervals: Wilson for accuracy [Wilson, 1927], Clopper–Pearson for the vendor’s statement [Clopper and Pearson, 1934], percentile bootstrap with 2,000 resamples for AUROC [Efron, 1979], and the exact McNemar test for paired differences [McNemar, 1947].

How the promise is measured.

A promise about accuracy among accepted items concerns the population the items come from, which is unknown. The idea is to let the 2,000 items stand in for that population and ask, over many calibration samples drawn from them, how often a rule picks a threshold whose accuracy on the whole population falls short. We measure it against a plug-in population under the exchangeability that every rule already assumes. The 2,000 items of a locale are taken as the population. A calibration sample of ncaln_{\text{cal}} items is drawn from it with replacement, the temperature (for Laya) and the threshold are fitted on the sample, and the true selective accuracy of the chosen threshold is computed on the whole population. A violation is a true selective accuracy below the target. Each rule is evaluated on 10,000 independent calibration draws, and the violation rate is reported with its one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson upper bound. To separate the uncertainty that comes from the items from Monte Carlo error, the same procedure is repeated on 200 bootstrap resamples of the items, each taken as a population. With p^b\hat{p}_{b} the rate on resample bb and M=1,000M=1{,}000 draws per resample, the Monte Carlo variance is w=1B​∑bp^b​(1−p^b)/(M−1)w=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b}\hat{p}_{b}(1-\hat{p}_{b})/(M-1), and the item variance is max⁡{0,Var^b​(p^b)−w}\max\{0,\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{b}(\hat{p}_{b})-w\}. The same split applies to decisions and to paired differences between rules, computed draw by draw. This checks the rules against the empirical distribution, and it is not a statement about the population behind the sample. Three properties of the construction bear on the numbers. A draw in which no threshold qualifies decides nothing and counts as a kept promise, so a rule can keep its rate low by abstaining, which is why decisions are reported next to every rate. A sample of 1,000 items drawn with replacement from 2,000 contains about 787 distinct items (about 442 for a sample of 500). And the population is discrete, so θ⁡(τ)\theta(\tau) is a step function of the threshold, coarsest for Jev, whose probabilities take few distinct values. The guarantee of Learn then Test assumes candidate thresholds fixed before the calibration data are seen. Here, as in common practice, the candidates are the observed confidences and the Laya temperature is fitted on the same sample, so the guarantee is approximate and the plug-in rates show how close it comes. The tolerance is fixed in advance at the nominal level of the rules: a rule passes when the upper bound of its violation rate is at most 0.05. The upper bound reflects Monte Carlo error only. The item-level standard deviation of the violation rates of the bounded rules reaches 0.016, and the mean over bootstrap populations differs from the plug-in value by up to 0.012, so differences of a point or two between rules are within what another sample of 2,000 items could produce. Because a rule whose true violation rate equals the nominal 5% would fail this tolerance about half of the time, single cases are also read in three categories, with a two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson interval on the violation rate: kept when its upper limit is at most 0.05, broken when its lower limit exceeds 0.05, and undetermined otherwise. Table 3 separates the levels that share the values 0.05 and 95%.

Reproducibility.

Every number in this paper is produced from the released items, the frozen Jev answers and the Laya probabilities per item by five scripts, all with the seed 20261020: metrics.py (accuracy, calibration, AUROC, costs and the curves of the figures), deletion.py (explanation fidelity), population_gate.py (the gate against the plug-in population), ablation_gate.py (the split-half ablation) and tables.py, which writes every table of the paper from their outputs, rounding half up on the stored values. Copies of the vendor documentation pages consulted on 2026-10-20 are archived with the data.

6 Results

6.1 Accuracy

Without fine-tuning, Jev is more accurate than every Laya checkpoint in both languages (Table 4). In Portuguese the three Laya checkpoints are indistinguishable from each other and about 21 points behind. With labels from the domain the order reverses: the fine-tuned multilingual checkpoint exceeds Jev by 2.6 points (p<0.001p<0.001). Three measurements of the fine-tune appear in the article and differ by recipe. The checkpoint of Table 4 is one fine-tune on the full partition with the recipe of the companion lesson (0.973). The label curve of Figure 1 comes from the same lesson, with three seeds per size. The paired measurement used for non-inferiority (Appendix B) refits with the recipe of the drift experiments and three seeds per size, and gives 0.947 at 4,000 labels and 0.962 at 11,274, 1.5 points above Jev, and the battery of Section 9 uses that recipe on its own grid up to 8,000 labels. The label curve in Figure 1 shows that about 4,000 labelled utterances reach Jev’s accuracy, in 17 seconds of training on one GPU, a measurement taken from the companion lesson repository with three seeds per size. The choice between the two models is thus less a matter of accuracy than of labels, language, privacy (Jev requires the state to leave the machine) and the need to audit.

Harder options.

The four distractors of an item are drawn from the other test intents, which rewards a decider that has learned how often each intent occurs. To measure that, the 2,000 items were rebuilt with the distractors drawn first from the gold intent’s scenario, 2.4 of the four on average (exploratory, registered before the run). Every decider loses accuracy: Jev 4.2 points in Portuguese and 3.9 in English, the released Laya checkpoints 12 to 20 points and the fine-tuned ones 4.5 and 5.2. With an empty utterance the fine-tuned checkpoints still answer 44% and 37% of the hard items correctly, against 20% by chance, and on the hard items their advantage over Jev lies entirely where the empty utterance already gives the answer: there it is 4.0 and 3.9 points, and where the empty utterance is wrong it is −0.2-0.2 ([−2.0,1.8][-2.0,1.8]) and −0.6-0.6 ([−2.3,1.2][-2.3,1.2]). The edge of the fine-tuned checkpoints over Jev comes from the frequency of the intents they learned, not from a better reading of the utterance.

What each route costs.

Jev needs no labels and costs US$0.016 per 1,000 decisions at the vendor’s price. Laya runs locally in about 12 ms per item on a CPU and is non-inferior to Jev from 4,000 labels on. The cost of each route, the break-even between labels and API spend, and the effect of the processor’s instruction set are in Appendix B.

6.2 Confidence as evidence

Ordering, not certifying.

No system reaches an AUROC of one (Table 6, Figure 2). Confidence orders cases: a correct answer drawn at random has higher confidence than a wrong one with probability between 0.80 and 0.96. It does not certify any single case. At confidence 0.97 or more, Jev still makes 6 errors among 819 answers in Portuguese and 5 among 862 in English, and the fine-tuned Laya 8 among 896.

A vendor statement, tested.

The vendor writes that outcomes assigned probability 1.0 “should occur 100% of the time” and that these rates “describe groups of predictions, not a guarantee about any single answer” [TypeSafe, 2026]. Jev’s probabilities are rounded to two decimals, so 1.00 means p≥0.995p\geq 0.995. In Portuguese, 724 of the 728 answers at 1.00 were correct, 99.45% with exact 95% interval [98.60%, 99.85%]. In English, 776 of 780. Read literally, “100%” is rejected, since the interval excludes one. Read with the rounding, it is compatible with calibration at p≥0.995p\geq 0.995. Each of these errors, alone, looked like certainty.

Calibration repaired, and its limits.

Temperature scaling repairs the global calibration of every Laya checkpoint, including the typed-decisions checkpoint, which is underconfident as returned (temperatures below one) and has the worst ECE as returned, 0.232 in English. Global calibration hides groups: in Portuguese the multilingual checkpoint has ECE 0.045 overall but 0.312 in the datetime scenario, and the median scenario ECE of the non-fine-tuned checkpoints is 2.8 to 3.3 times their global ECE in Portuguese and 1.8 to 2.9 times in English. Part of the gap is the upward bias of ECE in small groups, but the order of magnitude is the motivation for eq. 12.

6.3 The gate

F1 does not know what costs more.

The threshold that maximises the F1 of the gate on the calibration half accepts 97.2% of the reported items for Jev in Portuguese, with 39 type I and 14 type II errors, and 99.7% for the fine-tuned Laya, with 25 type I errors and one type II. Wherever a wrong action costs more than a review, this threshold is wrong by construction.

The Bayes threshold needs calibration.

Figure 3 shows the cost per item against the threshold for a cost ratio of 10:1 (τ∗=0.9\tau^{*}=0.9). For calibrated deciders the minimum lies near τ∗\tau^{*}, and the Bayes threshold, with no fitting, costs 0.248 per item for Jev against 0.234 for the threshold that minimises cost on the calibration half. For the multilingual Laya as returned, the same threshold costs 0.99 per item, against 0.79 after temperature scaling. At 100:1 the gap widens to 3.04 against 1.28. Two qualifications follow from the measurements. With an extreme ratio, the threshold fitted on the calibration half rests on a handful of errors and can be worse on new data than the Bayes threshold: 0.90 against 0.59 for the fine-tuned Laya at 100:1. And a single global temperature need not calibrate the tail where an extreme threshold sits: for Laya English in English at 100:1, the Bayes threshold costs 1.01 after temperature and 0.83 as returned. That difference rests on 5 against 1 accepted errors among 1,000 items, so it is suggestive rather than established, and the split-half evaluation of Section 6.4 points the same way: at that ratio, whose threshold is 0.99, the Bayes threshold breaks a promise of 99% in 29% of the splits for this checkpoint.

How the promise is measured.

The promise is measured against a plug-in population, as defined in Section 5.

Five rules for one promise.

Table 7 and Figure 4 compare the point rule, the ascending Beta rule, the same rule with the fixed-sequence scan, Learn then Test and SGR. Wherever the target binds, the point rule violates the promise in 39% to 53% of the calibration draws, the coin flip of Remark 1. Every rule built on a bound stays within the tolerance in every case, with 1,000 and with 500 calibration items, and the largest upper bound among them is 0.044. Their rates still differ. Learn then Test and the fixed-sequence Beta rule violate in at most 3.2% of the draws, SGR in at most 0.4% but decides about one item per 1,000 for Laya typed-decisions and Laya English in English at 99%, and the ascending Beta rule has the highest rate among the bounded rules, up to 3.7%. These results replicate, for typed deciders, the contrast between naive and certified thresholds reported for binary System One decisions [Messoudi and Mansar, 2026] and for signal detectors [Zhou and Wang, 2026], ablated across nine bound families on MASSIVE among other datasets [Basu, 2026], and seen on the Laya typed-decisions checkpoint itself, where a frozen point-estimate gate missed its error target and, in an exploratory analysis, a rule requiring a Wilson upper bound to clear the target brought the held-out error to 0.101 against a target of 0.10 [Nandakishore, 2026].

What the ascending scan buys, and at what price.

Table 8 isolates the difference to Learn then Test. The fixed-sequence Beta rule is Learn then Test with one pseudo-success (Remark 2): it decides at most 3.0 more items per 1,000 and violates at most 0.06 points more often. The ascending Beta rule differs by its ascending scan, and that is where both its gain and its cost come from. Read with the definitions of Section 4.7, both rules keep the promise in all 24 combinations of system, target and calibration size, so the ascending Beta rule is non-inferior to the tolerance wherever Learn then Test is. In no combination does it decide fewer items with an interval below zero, and it decides more, with a 95% interval that includes the item-level uncertainty above zero, in 4 of the 24. Two of these are clean gains, 1.1 more items per 1,000 for Jev in Portuguese at 95% with 500 calibration items and 28 more for the fine-tuned multilingual checkpoint at 99% (interval [6,51][6,51]), with no detectable change in violation. Two are trade-offs, 130 more for Laya typed-decisions in English at 99% ([27,233][27,233]) at a violation rate higher by 2.2 points ([0.8,3.7][0.8,3.7]), and 279 more for Laya English in English at 95% with 500 calibration items ([16,542][16,542]) at 1.4 points more ([0.1,2.7][0.1,2.7]), both still within the tolerance. The 24 combinations include both calibration sizes, and Table 8 shows the size of 1,000, where the same difference for Laya English has an item-level standard deviation of 172 and is not detected. In the other 20 combinations no difference in decisions is detected, and the item-level noise reaches 172 decisions per 1,000. With Holm’s correction over the 24 combinations, none of the four differences in decisions remains detected (scripts/holm.py). In the static setting, therefore, Learn then Test remains the rule that carries a guarantee, and the ascending Beta rule decides more items on average where the conditional accuracy is not monotone, a gain that the item-level uncertainty of this front does not confirm once the 24 comparisons are corrected for multiplicity.

The exchange rate.

Against the point rule, a bounded rule pays for each avoided wrong action with extra escalations. With the split-half evaluation of Appendix E, the ascending Beta rule spends about 14 extra reviews per avoided wrong action for the fine-tuned Laya, so it pays off as soon as a wrong action costs more than 14 reviews, as in an assistant that books events. For Jev, rounded probabilities create a step at 1.00 that leaves the rule without a qualifying threshold in 52% to 61% of the splits, and the rate rises to 78 to 92 reviews per avoided error, which pays off only for critical actions. Figure 5 places the splits on the accuracy–coverage plane: the point rule straddles the target line, the Beta rule moves left and up.

What lower coverage buys.

The curves of Figure 5 also show where escalating more is worth it. On the reported half in Portuguese, lowering the coverage from 100% to 90% removes 32 of Jev’s 53 errors at about 3 reviews per avoided error, and 19 of the 27 errors of the fine-tuned Laya at about 5. From 90% to 80% the price rises to about 6 and 25 reviews per avoided error, and below 80% almost nothing is left to avoid. Jev keeps 4 errors among the 728 answers it returns with probability 1.00, and the fine-tuned Laya reaches no error at 65% coverage, 650 items whose Beta lower bound is still only 0.995. The marginal price is the cost ratio at which each coverage is optimal, which is how Proposition 3 reads on data. A target of 99.5% asks for a coverage where each further error costs tens of reviews.

6.4 Why the bound works, and where it fails

To attribute the behaviour of the rules, we score 60 configurations on 1,000 random calibration/report splits of the 2,000 items (Appendix E). They cover:

  • •

    the point rule,

  • •

    the Beta rule with q∈{0.01,0.025,0.05,0.10,0.20}q\in\{0.01,0.025,0.05,0.10,0.20\}, the uniform, Jeffreys and Beta⁡(0,1)\mathrm{Beta}(0,1) priors and three scans, plus one variant with a minimum of 100 accepted items,

  • •

    Learn then Test and SGR with δ∈{0.01,0.05,0.10,0.20}\delta\in\{0.01,0.05,0.10,0.20\},

  • •

    the Bayes threshold for cost ratios of 10, 100 and 1,000,

  • •

    per-class thresholds with the point and the Beta rule.

The full grid runs with 1,000 calibration items at targets of 95% and 99%, with temperature scaling on and off for Laya. Jev is always used as returned. The core rules also run with 500 and 250 calibration items, at 99.5%, and on the non-fine-tuned checkpoints. The split-half rates include report-side noise. They serve to attribute effects, while the plug-in population above serves to judge the promise.

Why it works.

Almost the whole effect comes from replacing the point estimate by a bound. How much the prior weighs depends on which prior. Replacing the uniform prior of the rule by Beta⁡(0,1)\mathrm{Beta}(0,1) changes the split-half rate by at most 0.007 at q=0.05q=0.05, and against the plug-in population, with the definitions of Section 4.7, it keeps the promise in all 24 combinations of system, target and calibration size and changes decisions by at most 2.6 per 1,000. The Jeffreys prior, more liberal by half a pseudo-observation of each kind, decides more items in 16 combinations, by up to 245 per 1,000, but violates more often in 8 and breaks the promise in 5 of the 24, two with Jev, one with Laya typed-decisions and two with Laya English, all in English except one Jev case, and four of them at 99%, where the uniform prior keeps it. The prior is therefore not neutral. Priors at least as conservative as the uniform one keep the ascending scan within the tolerance at these sample sizes, and the Jeffreys prior does not. The credibility level qq acts as δ\delta does, with violation rates rising with qq. The bound also makes the rule abstain when the evidence is insufficient. With 250 calibration items at 99%, no bounded rule qualifies a threshold for any system, in agreement with Proposition 5, while the point rule still promises and breaks the promise in 50% to 65% of the splits. Every rule that counts accepted successes uses only the order of the confidences, so the point rule, the Beta rule, Learn then Test and SGR are nearly invariant to temperature scaling. For the fine-tuned multilingual checkpoint at 99%, the Beta rule gives 0.073 broken and 883 decisions after temperature scaling and 0.069 and 882 without. The invariance is not exact, because a temperature can reorder items whose probability vectors differ in shape: for Laya typed-decisions in English at 99%, the Beta rule decides 277 items per 1,000 after temperature scaling and 180 without.

Where it fails.

The ascending scan of the rule keeps the lowest threshold that qualifies anywhere, and so exploits stretches where the conditional accuracy is not monotone. This is the source of both its additional coverage and its failures in Tables 7 and 8. When qualification is rare, the chosen threshold is also optimistic. For Laya English in English at 99%, the calibration accuracy among accepted items exceeds the report accuracy by 1.2 points on average, against −0.1-0.1 to 0.40.4 points in the other eleven cases. Per-class thresholds either break the promise often or decide almost nothing. With 59 predicted intents, each class has about 17 calibration items, far below the minimum of Proposition 5: at 99%, the per-class point rule breaks the promise in 34% to 85% of the splits, and the per-class Beta rule decides no item.

When the ascending scan breaks the promise.

Proposition 4 locates every excess violation of the ascending scan in the draws where the two scans disagree, and the plug-in population measures it. Over 10,000 draws per combination, the fixed-sequence Beta rule violates within 0.0011 of Learn then Test in all 24 combinations, the scans disagree in 0% to 60% of the draws, and the inclusion of part (ii) holds in every combination. Disagreement alone is not the danger. Where the ascending threshold covers about as much as the fixed-sequence one, the disagreeing draws violate no more often than the others, as for Laya English in English at 95%, which disagrees in 59% of the draws. The danger is a jump in coverage. In the three combinations where the disagreeing draws cover more than 10 points above the rest, 0.91 to 0.95 against 0.74 to 0.80, the promise breaks in 17% to 98% of them (the fine-tuned checkpoints at 99% with 500 calibration items, and Jev in English at 99%). The ascending scan therefore fails where the accuracy–coverage curve of Figure 5 flattens near the target at high coverage, and a deployment can detect the risk by comparing the two scans on its own calibration sample.

Across every evaluation.

The tolerance used so far counts a promise as kept only when the upper bound of its violation rate is at most 0.05, so a rule whose true rate equals the nominal 5% would fail about half of the time. A fairer reading sorts each evaluation into three categories with a two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson interval: kept when the upper bound is at most 0.05, broken when the lower bound exceeds 0.05, and undetermined otherwise. Table 9 applies it to the 190 evaluations of this article in which calibration and evaluation items are exchangeable: the static gate of this section, the same design for the three released checkpoints in Portuguese, the battery of Section 9 with MASSIVE pt-PT as its reference, and Laya calibrated on each MASSIVE locale. Every case left undetermined with 2,000 draws was run again with 10,000. Against the point rule, the usual choice when no guarantee is sought, the ascending Beta rule always pays: the point rule breaks the promise in 147 of the 190 cases with mean violation rates of 29% to 48%, and the Beta rule brings them to 1.5% to 2.7% at a cost of 51 to 165 decisions per 1,000. Against Learn then Test, which keeps the promise in all 190 cases, the Beta rule decides more items on average in 128 cases and fewer in none, differences between means over calibration draws that do not include the uncertainty of the items, 16 more per 1,000 for Jev, 34 for the fine-tuned Laya and 73 for Laya as released, almost twice as many. Its price is a violation rate near the nominal level without a guarantee: the mean rises from 1.0% to 1.7% for Learn then Test to 1.5% to 2.7%, six cases are undetermined, and one is broken, the fine-tuned checkpoint calibrated in Armenian at 5.5% (95% interval [5.1,6.0][5.1,6.0]). In every case where the Beta rule exceeds the nominal level, the two scans disagree in 64% to 79% of the draws, as Proposition 4 anticipates. The Beta rule is therefore the better trade when more automatic decisions matter more than a formal guarantee, and it gains most with the weakest decider. Where the promise needs a guarantee, Learn then Test remains the rule.

Checked on new items.

The plug-in population treats the 2,000 items as the population. To check that reading, the gate was calibrated on the same kind of draws and read both on the sample and on 2,989 Portuguese and 3,003 English MASSIVE items outside it, the dev partition and the test rows not sampled, with Jev called again so that its answers carry the variation of the API (exploratory, registered before the run). In four of the six cases the new items confirm the plug-in reading: the point rule breaks the promise in 35% to 51% of the draws where it broke on the sample, and the bounded rules stay at or below 3.8%. In the other two the bounded rules break on the new items, Learn then Test included. The fine-tuned multilingual checkpoint, whose accuracy falls from 0.975 on the sample to 0.965 on the new items, breaks a promise of 99% in 30% of the draws under Learn then Test and 41% under the Beta rule. Laya English, with a similar accuracy on both (0.886 and 0.893) but a confidence that ranks the new items differently, breaks a promise of 95% in 6.1% and 10.9% of the draws. A guarantee for exchangeable items does not survive a shift as small as the one from the sampled test rows to the dev partition, and the lower accuracy of the fine-tuned checkpoint on new items is consistent with the near duplicates noted in the limitations.

7 When the input is noisy

Every measurement so far uses MASSIVE as written, clean and in lower case. Real messages arrive with typing errors, words out of order and, in Portuguese, without accents. Clean training data of this kind is, in effect, combed, and it does not prepare a decider for the wild. The question for a caller is whether such noise changes the decisions and whether the promise of a gate calibrated on clean text survives it. Five operators were applied to the report items, deterministic given a seed: keyboard typos (a QWERTY neighbour, a deleted, a doubled or two transposed letters) hitting 5%, 10% or 20% of the words, adjacent words swapped, lower case without punctuation, accents removed, and a mixed profile that combines the last three with typos. Laya, as released and fine-tuned, and Jev 1.13, through the API with fresh answers for clean and noisy text alike (19,000 calls, US$0.31), were measured on every condition. All of this is exploratory, registered before the runs.

Accuracy degrades, unevenly.

Paired against clean text with an item bootstrap, typos and the mixed profile cost Jev 0.7 to 2.2 points of accuracy on average, and removing accents costs it nothing detectable (Table 10). The fine-tuned Laya loses 2.4 to 5.7 points and the released checkpoint 4.6 to 9.6. Swapping adjacent words and dropping punctuation change almost nothing for any of them. Fine-tuning on clean labels made Laya 2.3 points more accurate than Jev on clean Portuguese text and 1.2 points on clean English text, and noise shrinks the difference to between −2.7-2.7 and +0.5+0.5 points, Jev being ahead by 2.7 under the heaviest mixed noise in English.

The promise does not travel.

A threshold chosen on clean items keeps the promise of 95% on clean report items for every system, and breaks it on noisy ones. For the fine-tuned Laya the promise breaks in 11 of the 12 typo and mixed conditions of the two languages, with violation rates of 95% to 100%, and for Jev in 9 of the 12, with rates of 13% to 81%, by the Beta rule and by Learn then Test alike. A loss of a few points of accuracy is enough, because it falls on the accepted items and pushes their accuracy below the target. This is the failure of exchangeability that the drift streams of Section 10 also meet, produced here by nothing more than ordinary typing.

A few typos flip confident decisions.

A greedy search that applies, one at a time, the typo that most lowers the probability of the clean decision changes the decision of the fine-tuned Laya on 27.5% of 200 Portuguese items with a single typo (95% interval [21,34][21,34]), 59% with two and 77.5% with three, and of the released checkpoint on 69%, 88% and 96%. English is similar. The confidence gives no warning. Among the decisions flipped, the median probability of the clean decision was 0.9999, and in Portuguese 88% of them had a probability of at least 0.99. Figure 6 shows both sides, and Table 11 shows what such an attack looks like.

Training with noise is a gain of method.

The fine-tuning recipe of the original head, with half of the training items passed through a random operator, keeps the clean accuracy and raises the noisy one. Against the same recipe without noise, paired over items and averaged over three seeds, the clean accuracy is non-inferior with the 2-point margin of Section 4.7 (Portuguese +0.3+0.3 with interval [−0.1,0.8][-0.1,0.8], English +0.3+0.3 with interval [−0.2,0.8][-0.2,0.8]), and the accuracy under the mixed profile at 10%, the condition fixed in advance, is higher (+1.6+1.6, [0.7,2.4][0.7,2.4], and +0.8+0.8, [0.1,1.5][0.1,1.5]). By the protocol of Section 4.7 this is superiority on noisy text with non-inferiority on clean text, at no cost in labels, not an efficiency gain, which would require a resource saved. It recovers about half of what noise takes in Portuguese, from 0.930 to 0.946 under the mixed profile against 0.964 on clean text.

For a caller, the reading is direct. A gate is calibrated for the inputs it was calibrated on, and typing noise is enough to break it, so the calibration items must look like the traffic, noise included. Fine-tuning for accuracy should add noise to its training data, which costs nothing on clean text. And a probability of 0.9999 does not certify that a decision would survive a single typo.

8 When the language changes

Noise is one change of the input that a deployment meets. Language is another, and a decider offered as multilingual invites the question of whether a promise calibrated in one language holds in the others. MASSIVE 1.1 gives the same utterances in 52 locales [FitzGerald et al., 2023]. Each of the 2,000 items of the article was mapped to its MASSIVE identifier, and the utterance with the same identifier replaced the Portuguese one in every locale, with the options and the gold intent kept, so the items are parallel across locales. Jev 1.13 answered the 1,000 report items of the 50 locales not measured before (50,000 calls, US$0.83), and Laya multilingual answered all items as released and as fine-tuned in Portuguese. The analysis was registered before the runs and is exploratory. A deployment that starts in English calibrates in English. The threshold is therefore chosen on the 1,000 calibration items of en-US, with the temperature fitted on the same draw for Laya, and applied to the report items of each locale, which share no item with the calibration items. The check is the plug-in procedure of Section 6.3 with 2,000 draws, run by the tool released with the article (promise_check), whose test reproduces the plug-in results of Section 6.3 within four standard errors.

Accuracy.

Jev loses 0.3 to 9.4 points against en-US, most in Javanese, Swahili, Khmer and Welsh, and is non-inferior to en-US with the 2-point margin of Section 4.7 in 6 of the 51 locales. The released Laya loses 1.4 to 47.2 points and is non-inferior in none. Its median loss is 20.7 points in the 23 locales not written in Latin script and 12.4 in the 28 that are, a descriptive contrast, since no grouping was tested. Fine-tuning in Portuguese raises Laya’s accuracy in every locale, by 14.9 to 30.5 points with every lower bound above 11.7, so the labels of one language help all the others measured. The fine-tuned checkpoint still loses up to 40.2 points (Amharic) and is non-inferior to en-US only in pt-PT, the language it was tuned on. Table 23 in Appendix F gives every locale, and a machine-readable copy is released with the data.

Calibration error stays low, and the promise does not travel.

Jev’s ECE stays between 0.009 and 0.030 in every locale, against 0.016 on the en-US items of this front, in line with the stable calibration error that Fadli et al. [2026] report for Jev on Indonesian regional languages. The promise does not follow it. Calibrated in en-US, the promise of 95% holds in 8 of the 51 locales for Jev, by the point rule, the Beta rule and Learn then Test alike, and breaks in the other 43 with violation rates of 0.31 to 1.00 (Figure 7). The reason is arithmetic. At 95% Jev accepts more than 99% of the items in en-US, whose accuracy among accepted items is 96.2%, so the promise has a slack of 1.2 points. Every locale that loses at most 1.1 points keeps it, and every locale that loses 1.2 points or more breaks it, with a Spearman correlation of −0.95-0.95 between the loss and the violation rate. The released Laya keeps the promise calibrated in English only in Japanese, and the fine-tuned checkpoint in six locales, pt-PT, es-ES, fr-FR, it-IT, ja-JP and zh-CN. Ahuja et al. [2022] found multilingual encoders miscalibrated in low-resource languages and in languages typologically distant from English, and found temperature scaling and a few examples in the language helpful. The measurements here add that a well calibrated probability is not enough. What has to travel is the threshold, and it travels only as far as the slack of the promise allows.

Calibrating in each language.

Laya can be calibrated on the 1,000 calibration items of each locale and checked on its report items. The released checkpoint then keeps the promise in 3 of the 51 locales with the point rule, in 29 with the Beta rule and in 35 with Learn then Test, at median decisions per 1,000 of 257, 119 and 45. The fine-tuned checkpoint keeps it in 9, 18 and 20, at 814, 757 and 752.
