This check evaluates one fixed report half rather than a plug-in population, so a locale whose accepted items are few is judged on a small sample, and the counts carry that variability. The pattern is nonetheless that of Section 6.3, repeated over 51 languages: a bound keeps the promise where the point estimate breaks it, and pays for it in decisions, most where the decider is weakest.

For a caller, a decider that serves several languages needs a calibration sample in each of them. A low ECE in every language does not replace it, and neither does a small loss of accuracy. The slack of the promise in the calibration language, the accuracy among accepted items minus the target, is the loss of accuracy that a promise can absorb, and here it was about one point.

9 When the domain changes

Every measurement so far uses intents from MASSIVE. To see which findings belong to the method and which to that dataset, the same code was run on four further domains, registered before any answer was collected and exploratory throughout. News Category headlines [Misra, 2022] ask for one of five categories drawn from 42. Financial tweets ask whether a tweet is bearish, bullish or neutral (Twitter Financial News sentiment, MIT licence, https://huggingface.co/datasets/zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment). LIAR2 [Xu and Kechadi, 2024] asks for the fact-checker’s rating of a political claim on six levels, from the statement alone. Fake.Br [Monteiro et al., 2018] asks whether a Portuguese news text is fake or real. Its size-normalised texts pair each fake item with a true one on the same topic, and pairs were drawn whole so that no topic is split between the items and the training data. FakeRecogna [Garcia et al., 2022], planned for this slot, was replaced before any answer was collected, because 71% of its fake items carry a verdict marker such as “#boato” in the title, against 1.4% of its real items. Each domain gives 2,000 items, half for calibration and half for report. Jev 1.13 answered every item, the report items under typos and the mixed profile at 10%, and the empty state (17,003 calls, US$0.30). Laya multilingual answered as released and after fine-tuning on 250 to 8,000 labelled items of the domain with three seeds, 32 to 43 seconds of training for the largest size on one GPU. Table 12 gives the reading across domains, Figure 8 the label curves and Appendix G one report card per domain.

Labels decide the comparison, and the domain decides the labels.

The fine-tune is more accurate than Jev from 250 labels on financial tweets and on Fake.Br, reaching 0.926 against 0.728 and 0.981 against 0.716. On news headlines it needs 8,000 labels to be non-inferior and is not detectably more accurate. On LIAR2 it is never non-inferior, and neither model moves far from always answering “false”, which is right for 28.5% of the report items. The 4,000 labels of MASSIVE are therefore a property of that task, not a constant of the method, and the label curve has to be measured in the domain at hand.

Calibration does not travel either.

Jev’s ECE, 0.020 on MASSIVE in Portuguese, the reference row of the battery, is 0.076 on news headlines, 0.087 on Fake.Br, 0.162 on LIAR2 and 0.171 on financial tweets, where 0.82 of confidence goes with 0.60 of accuracy among the most confident LIAR2 decisions. Laya after the temperature fitted on the calibration half stays between 0.006 and 0.048. A calibration measured on one task licenses nothing about another, and the temperature, fitted on a few hundred labelled items of the domain, is the cheap repair.

The gate.

Across the four domains, the point rule keeps the promise in 20 of 40 cases and the bounded rules in most: Learn then Test in 39 and the Beta rule in 35. The five Beta cases outside the tolerance have estimated violation rates of 0.042 to 0.050, above 0.05 only by the upper bound of 2,000 draws, and four of them are fine-tunes on news headlines or financial tweets. At 0.95 the fine-tunes decide a median of 517 items per 1,000 with the Beta rule against 331 with Learn then Test on news headlines, and 842 against 532 on financial tweets. The trade measured on MASSIVE recurs: more decisions for a tolerated excess of risk that sits at the tolerance, not beyond it.

Typos break the promise again.

Calibrated on clean text, the 0.95 promise of the fine-tune breaks under typos in every seed on news headlines and financial tweets, with violation rates of 0.21 to 0.92. Jev’s promise breaks as well where Jev decides, 0.20 at 0.95 and 0.50 at 0.90 on news headlines, although its accuracy under typos changes by −0.5-0.5 points with an interval containing zero. As on MASSIVE, a loss too small to detect in accuracy is enough to break a promise that sits on the accepted items. On Fake.Br typos cost nothing, but the mixed profile drops the fine-tune by 34 to 40 points and breaks its promise in every draw, which the next paragraph explains.

What the fine-tune read in Fake.Br.

Three tests registered after this result separate form from content. Removing punctuation alone costs the fine-tune 34.3 points (95% interval [31.4,37.2][31.4,37.2]), while lower case costs 0.7, removing accents 0.4 and typos 0.5. A logistic regression on surface features only, with no word in it, reaches 0.807 ([0.781,0.830][0.781,0.830]): fake items carry more quotation marks, exclamation marks and full stops, true items more commas and hyphens. And Laya fine-tuned on text without punctuation or capitals still reaches 0.931 on such text. The wording carries most of the signal, and the fine-tune leaned on punctuation because the training data offered it, which a validation split from the same source cannot reveal. Removing the form from the training data costs 7 points on the original text (0.909 against 0.983) and keeps 0.931 on text without it, where the original fine-tune falls to 0.606, the same exchange as the training with noise of Section 7.

The empty state follows the training labels.

On news headlines, whose options change from item to item, the fine-tune answers 0.32 to 0.37 of the report items correctly with an empty state, against 0.17 before fine-tuning and 0.23 for Jev, and picks the most frequent training category among the options in 45% to 48% of the items, the pattern of MASSIVE. Where the options are fixed, the empty state yields one answer for all items: the majority class for every model on financial tweets (neutral, 64.5%), and on LIAR2 “false” for Jev and two of the three fine-tunes.

When no promise can be made.

On LIAR2 no rule accepts a single item at 0.90 or 0.95, and Proposition 6 gives a reason compatible with this: no rule can promise more than the accuracy the input allows. Among the 20 most confident report items Jev is right in 45% and the fine-tunes in 60% to 65%, so no threshold isolates a group that reaches 90%. The authors of LIAR2 report 0.32 for the statement alone with their own model trained on the full training split, the accuracy reached here, which is compatible with a low ceiling for that input, though the ceiling itself is not observed. The measures that follow were taken after this result and are exploratory. Better estimates move a decider towards the ceiling: the mean of Jev’s and the fine-tunes’ probabilities is right in 0.349 of the report items and in 67% of its 100 most confident, against 50% and 60% for each alone. More information in the state can raise the ceiling, but only if it is informative and clean. The speaker record published with LIAR2 counts the rating of the statement itself, which is at least one in every row, so it was replaced by the record of the speaker in a disjoint half of the training split. A record that left out only the row itself let the fine-tunes identify training labels through the speaker and was not used. With the clean record in a structured state, accuracy changes by +2.1+2.1 points for Jev ([−0.6,4.8][-0.6,4.8]) and by −2.5-2.5 to +1.7+1.7 for the fine-tunes, all with intervals containing zero. A coarser question raises the ceiling at once: on two levels, the false side against the true side, whose majority is 0.577, the 100 most confident decisions are right in 95% to 97% of the items, so a promise of 90% becomes possible for a tenth of them, on a question that no longer asks for the rating. And a set-valued answer always keeps its promise: split conformal sets cover the rating in 89% to 91% of the report items at the 90% level, with 3.9 to 4.6 of the six ratings in a set. The size of the set is the measure of how little the statement says.

For a caller, the battery turns the findings of MASSIVE into checks that a deployment can run in its own domain with promise_check: the label curve against the closed model, the calibration of each model on the domain, the gate with a bounded rule, the promise under the noise the traffic will carry, a test of what the fine-tune reads, and the ceiling of the promise when no rule decides.

10 When a Bayesian retraining loop is useful under drift

Every rule of Section 6.3 assumes that the items used to choose the threshold and the items the gate later decides are exchangeable. A deployed decider loses that assumption when its inputs or the meaning of its labels change [Gama et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2018], and the promise of the gate then has to be kept by watching it, retraining when it breaks and qualifying the threshold again. Deciding to act only when a change harms the deployed model, rather than whenever the inputs move, is the question of sequential risk tracking [Podkopaev and Ramdas, 2022]. A Bayesian loop for the three steps is studied here. Its online update, exponential forgetting of Beta evidence with the Laplace predictive, is the Beta reputation system of Jøsang and Ismail [2002], the update of discounted Thompson sampling [Raj and Kalyani, 2017] and the binomial case of the discount-factor dynamic models of West and Harrison [1997], and what the loop adds is its coupling to the acceptance gate, with a trigger that chooses between retraining and re-qualifying the threshold. This section asks when that loop is useful compared with the state-of-the-art alternatives for the same task, measured on streams with a known change, under a preregistration frozen before any pilot run. Every implementation choice the preregistration left open was recorded before the run it affects.

10.1 The loop and its comparators

The decider is the multilingual Laya checkpoint on five-option intent questions built as in Section 5, with the promise of an accuracy of at least α=0.95\alpha=0.95 among the items it decides alone and q=δ=0.05q=\delta=0.05. Labels come from two sources, each at the cost of one review: every escalated item, and a uniform audit of 5% of the accepted items. Escalated items are selected by low confidence and misrepresent the error rate among accepted items, so the drift monitors read the audit labels only, while promotion and re-qualification use all labels.

The loop has three Beta steps.

  • •

    Trigger. The audited accepted items give a Beta posterior of the accuracy among accepted items, with counts discounted by a factor λ\lambda per window of 500 items, and retraining starts when P⁡(θ<α)≥1−qP(\theta<\alpha)\geq 1-q.

  • •

    Promotion. The retrained and the current model are compared on a hold-out of recent labelled items, and the new model replaces the current one when P⁡(new better)≥1−qP(\text{new better})\geq 1-q under Beta⁡(b+1,c+1)\mathrm{Beta}(b+1,c+1) on the bb and cc discordant pairs.

  • •

    Re-qualification. The threshold is chosen again with the Beta lower-bound rule of Section 4.5.

Eight comparators share the decider, the retraining procedure, the audit rate and the label stream. The frozen model never retrains. The periodic arm retrains every KK items. Recalibration only re-estimates the accuracy per confidence bin by Laplace’s rule of succession. DDM [Gama et al., 2004], ADWIN [Bifet and Gavaldà, 2007] and Page–Hinkley [Page, 1954] watch the audited error stream, with promotion always, by the exact McNemar test [Dietterich, 1998] or by the high-confidence safety test of Thomas et al. [2019], as tuning options. Two arms never retrain and only move the threshold, Learn then Test qualified again in every window and adaptive conformal inference (ACI) [Gibbs and Candès, 2021]. Every retrain fine-tunes the current model for two epochs on the most recent 4,000 labelled items with 20% replay of the initial training set, and the arms that do not use the Beta rule re-qualify with Learn then Test.

10.2 Streams and measures

Three synthetic drifts are built from MASSIVE. In D1, five of the 18 scenarios, drawn before freezing, are absent from the initial training and enter the stream after the change, a knock-out shift reversed [Rabanser et al., 2018]. In D2, the language changes from Portuguese to English on parallel items. In D3, two pairs of intents, also drawn before freezing, swap their labels, a change of concept rather than of inputs. Each stream has 9,000 items, with the change at a point drawn uniformly between items 3,000 and 5,000, abrupt or gradual over 1,000 items [Gama et al., 2014]. A stream without drift measures false retrains. Thirty replicates per drift and pattern give 1,890 runs over the nine arms. The real streams use the News Category Dataset [Misra, 2022], HuffPost headlines from 2012 to 2022 whose earlier years form the HuffPost part of Wild-Time [Yao et al., 2022]. Each of ten transitions between consecutive years is a stream family with five random orders and the change on 1 January. Temporal change does not always degrade a model [Agarwal and Nenkova, 2022], so a transition counts only if the frozen model loses at least 2 points of accuracy across it.

The primary measure is the cost per item at a cost ratio of 10, where a wrong automatic action costs 10 and each escalation and each audit label costs 1, with retraining free in the primary analysis and costing 50 in a sensitivity analysis. The promise is checked on the true selective accuracy of each post-change window, measured on the test split reweighted to the stream’s current mixture. Twenty configurations per arm were tuned on separate streams. The loop selected λ=0.95\lambda=0.95 and q=0.01q=0.01, both at the edge of the preregistered grid, and the best comparator was the periodic arm with K=3,000K=3{,}000 and promotion always, at a tuning cost of 0.618 against 0.611 for the loop.

The loop counts as useful, which is the claim the preregistration ties to the title, if its cost is lower than the best comparator’s with a paired 95% interval excluding zero in at least two of the three drifts, if the share of post-change windows below α\alpha exceeds the comparator’s by at most 0.02, and if it shows no more false retrains on the control stream. The real streams are supporting evidence. In the main run, the true selective accuracy of the frozen model moves by +0.1+0.1 points across the language change of D2, against −6.0-6.0 for D1 and −9.5-9.5 for D3, so D2 is read as a drift that does not degrade the model. The pilot value for D2 is not used, because the pilot cached encodings by item identifier and MASSIVE gives the same identifier to an utterance in every locale. The main run keys the cache by content.

10.3 Results

By the preregistered rule, the loop does not improve on the best comparator selected in tuning, the periodic arm (Table 13). Paired over the 60 streams of each drift, its cost is higher in D1 by 0.044 (95% interval [0.002,0.087][0.002,0.087]) and in D3 by 0.020 ([0.004,0.035][0.004,0.035]), and lower only in D2, by 0.064 ([−0.079,−0.049][-0.079,-0.049]). Non-inferiority on the windows below the promise holds in D2 and fails in D1 (difference 0.034, upper bound 0.113) and D3 (0.305, upper bound 0.387). On the control stream the loop never retrains, against three retrains of the periodic arm. The preregistered sensitivity analysis charges 50 reviews per retrain. Under it the difference against the periodic arm is no longer detected in D1 (0.033, [−0.009,0.075][-0.009,0.075]) or D3 (0.010, [−0.006,0.025][-0.006,0.025]), and the loop is cheaper by 0.081 in D2 and 0.066 on the control stream (both intervals below −0.04-0.04), so where retraining has a real cost the loop is no longer detectably more expensive than the periodic arm on any stream type, which is not the same as equivalent. The claim the preregistration ties to the title is therefore not supported, and the title does not make it.

The question of when the loop is useful has a sharper answer than the rule. The loop pays off where the stream does not degrade the model. On the control stream and on D2, the change of language that costs the frozen model almost nothing, it has the lowest mean cost of the nine arms, 0.433 and 0.402, because it does not retrain where there is nothing to repair, while the periodic arm retrains three times and DDM between 1.5 and 2 times. Against recalibration only and Learn then Test per window, which do not retrain either, no difference in cost is detected. Where the drift degrades the model, the loop reacts late and little. Its median first retrain comes 1,924 items after the change in D1 and 2,792 in D3, with 0.9 and 1.2 retrains per stream, and 86% and 93% of the post-change windows stay below the promise. The trigger reads only the audited accepted items, about 25 per window, and it asks for a posterior probability of at least 0.99 that the promise is broken. No arm that retrains keeps the promise under D1 or D3. The periodic arm, the best of them, still leaves 83% and 62% of the windows below α\alpha, with three retrains and three promotions per stream.

The arms that do best under a degrading drift move only the threshold. Learn then Test qualified again in every window has the lowest cost in D1 and D3 and the fewest windows below the promise, 37% and 21%, and it pays for this in reviews, with 302 and 572 labels per 1,000 items against 110 and 133 for the loop. At a cost ratio of 100 it is the cheapest arm on all four stream types. Paired with the loop, as an exploratory comparison, its cost is lower by 0.096 in D1 ([0.067,0.126][0.067,0.126]) and by 0.052 in D3 ([0.036,0.068][0.036,0.068]), with intervals containing zero in D2 and on the control stream. This arm ranked last in tuning, on shorter streams of 4,000 items that change earlier, so it was not the preregistered comparator, and whether the length of the tuning streams explains the reversal was not tested. Recalibration alone, sits between the two in D1 and D3 and is close to the loop where nothing degrades.

The comparison protocol of Section 4.7 makes the trade explicit (Table 14). Where the stream does not degrade the model, the loop is a clean efficiency gain over the periodic arm and DDM, with the same or a better promise and no retrains, and it is equivalent to recalibration only. Against Learn then Test per window it saves 94 labels per 1,000 items in D2 and 97 on the control stream at equal promise, but accepts 8 and 9 more wrong actions per 1,000, a trade-off. Under D1 and D3 it is not non-inferior to the periodic arm, to recalibration only or to Learn then Test per window. Recalibration only, Laplace’s rule per bin with forgetting, is non-inferior to every arm except Learn then Test per window under D1 and D3, never retrains, and is a clean gain over the periodic arm and DDM on the stable streams. With Holm’s correction over the 64 comparisons, 19 of the 27 gains remain. The eight lost are against DDM and Page–Hinkley, and every gain of the loop and of recalibration over the periodic arm on the stable streams remains. Under degradation its gains are trade-offs, fewer retrains and less GPU time paid with more labels, 190 more per 1,000 items than the loop in D1.

For a caller, the reading is the following. When the stream is stable or its change is harmless, the loop avoids needless retraining at the lowest cost measured. When the change degrades the model and escalation is affordable, re-qualifying the threshold every window keeps the promise more often than any retraining arm, at the price of more reviews. Even the best arm leaves 37% of the post-change windows of D1 below the promise, so a degrading drift of this size calls for a human decision on the model, not only for an automatic loop.

Which component drives the loop.

The attribution ablation swaps one component of the loop at a time on the same 60 streams per drift, and credits a component when swapping it raises the cost with an interval above zero. Only the trigger is credited. Replacing the posterior under the uniform prior by the one-sided Clopper–Pearson bound on the same counts makes the loop retrain less, 0.6 and 0.8 fewer times per stream, and raises its cost by 0.046 in D1 ([0.025,0.066][0.025,0.066]) and 0.012 in D3 ([0.006,0.017][0.006,0.017]). The other three components work against the loop. Counting per window instead of discounting lowers the cost in D1 by 0.048 ([−0.068,−0.029][-0.068,-0.029]), with 0.7 more retrains per stream. Promoting every retrained model lowers it in D1 by 0.019 and in D3 by 0.008, so the Beta test on discordant pairs rejects useful models. Re-qualifying the threshold with Learn then Test leaves the cost unchanged but lowers the share of post-change windows below the promise by 6 points in D1, with an upper bound just below zero, and by 22 points in D3 ([−30,−14][-30,-14]). The weak link of the loop is therefore its last step. After a promotion, the threshold is chosen again on the most recent labels, which over-represent escalated, hard items, and the ascending scan of the Beta rule is exactly the procedure that Proposition 4 shows to lose its guarantee when the qualification pattern is not monotone. In D2 no swap changes the cost by more than 0.001.

Repairing the re-qualification.

A second ablation, designed after the first and reported in Appendix D, tests repairs of the weak step. Re-qualifying on items held out of the retraining set repairs the loop on D1, and the fixed-sequence scan and weights for the probability of being labelled repair it on D3.

10.4 When the drift has a pattern

The loop and the recalibration arm track the accuracy of each confidence bin with a forgetting Beta, a local-level model that can follow a change only after it has happened. Many deployments meet changes that recur or announce themselves: traffic that alternates between languages, noise that rises at some hours, an input feature that shifts before the accuracy does. A dynamic generalised linear model with binomial observations [West et al., 1985; West and Harrison, 1997] keeps the per-bin tracking and lets trend, seasonality and inputs enter, so that the gate can use the accuracy predicted for the next window instead of the accuracy estimated for the last one.

The model.

For confidence bin bb and window tt, let θb,t\theta_{b,t} be the accuracy of the items in the bin and ηb,t=logit⁡θb,t\eta_{b,t}=\operatorname{logit}\theta_{b,t}. The state βb,t\beta_{b,t} holds a level, a harmonic pair of known period PP and the coefficients of window inputs xtx_{t} computed from the texts alone,

ηb,t=Ft⊤βb,t,βb,t=Gβb,t−1+ωb,t,yb,t∣θb,t∼Bin(nb,t,θb,t),\eta_{b,t}=F_{t}^{\top}\beta_{b,t},\qquad\beta_{b,t}=G\,\beta_{b,t-1}+\omega_{b,t},\qquad y_{b,t}\mid\theta_{b,t}\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n_{b,t},\theta_{b,t}), (13)

with Ft=(1,1,0,xt⊤)⊤F_{t}=(1,1,0,x_{t}^{\top})^{\top}, GG block diagonal with 11, the rotation by 2​π/P2\pi/P and the identity, and the evolution variance set by component discount factors, so that the prior variance of the state is Rt=Δ−1/2GCt−1G⊤Δ−1/2R_{t}=\Delta^{-1/2}GC_{t-1}G^{\top}\Delta^{-1/2} with Δ\Delta the diagonal of discounts. Given the prior moments f=Ft⊤​atf=F_{t}^{\top}a_{t} and q=Ft⊤​Rt​Ftq=F_{t}^{\top}R_{t}F_{t} of ηb,t\eta_{b,t}, conjugate updating [West et al., 1985] represents the prior of θb,t\theta_{b,t} by the Beta whose logit has these moments,

ψ⁡(r)−ψ⁡(s)=f,ψ′​(r)+ψ′​(s)=q,\psi(r)-\psi(s)=f,\qquad\psi^{\prime}(r)+\psi^{\prime}(s)=q, (14)

with ψ\psi the digamma function, updates it to Beta⁡(r+y,s+n−y)\mathrm{Beta}(r+y,\,s+n-y) with the labels of the window, and returns to the state through the posterior moments (f∗,q∗)(f^{*},q^{*}) of the logit: mt=at+Rt​Ft​(f∗−f)/qm_{t}=a_{t}+R_{t}F_{t}(f^{*}-f)/q and Ct=Rt−Rt​Ft​Ft⊤​Rt​(1−q∗/q)/qC_{t}=R_{t}-R_{t}F_{t}F_{t}^{\top}R_{t}(1-q^{*}/q)/q. West, Harrison and Migon solve eq. 14 by r=(1+ef)/qr=(1+e^{f})/q and s=(1+e−f)/qs=(1+e^{-f})/q, which is accurate only for small qq. With a few labels per bin and window, as an audit of 5% split into 20 bins gives, qq stays near one, the approximation returns s<1s<1, and every window without an error pushes the logit up without bound. The adapter therefore solves eq. 14 exactly by Newton’s method.

The gate.

Before window tt is gated, its inputs xtx_{t} are computed and each bin receives its one-step-ahead predictive Beta⁡(rb,t,sb,t)\mathrm{Beta}(r_{b,t},s_{b,t}). The set AtA_{t} of accepted bins holds the bins whose predictive qbq_{b}-quantile is at least α\alpha, for a fixed level qbq_{b} per bin, or, in the variant that matches the recalibration arm, whose predictive mean rb,t/(rb,t+sb,t)r_{b,t}/(r_{b,t}+s_{b,t}) is. When AtA_{t} is empty the gate acts on nothing in window tt and the promise holds vacuously. The lower-bound variant run in the experiments uses qb=0.05q_{b}=0.05 in every bin.

Proposition 7 (When the dynamic gate keeps the promise).

Let wb,t≥0w_{b,t}\geq 0 be the share of the items of window tt that fall in bin bb, and Θt=∑b∈Atwb,t​θb,t/∑b∈Atwb,t\Theta_{t}=\sum_{b\in A_{t}}w_{b,t}\theta_{b,t}/\sum_{b\in A_{t}}w_{b,t} the accuracy among accepted items.

  1. (i)

    If θb,t≥α\theta_{b,t}\geq\alpha for every b∈Atb\in A_{t}, then Θt≥α\Theta_{t}\geq\alpha. The condition is sufficient, not necessary.

  2. (ii)

    If eq. 13 holds as a Bayesian model and every bin is gated at level qb=q/Bq_{b}=q/B, with BB the number of bins, then, whenever AtA_{t} is non-empty, ℙ⁡(Θt≥α∣labels up to ​t−1​ and inputs up to ​t)≥1−q\mathbb{P}(\Theta_{t}\geq\alpha\mid\text{labels up to }t-1\text{ and inputs up to }t)\geq 1-q. The run with qb=0.05q_{b}=0.05 controls each bin, not their mixture.

  3. (iii)

    With the level alone, a single discount λ\lambda and exact moment matching, and to first order in 1/r1/r and 1/s1/s, one window of evolution and updating maps (r,s)(r,s) to (λ​r+y,λ​s+n−y)(\lambda r+y,\ \lambda s+n-y), the forgetting Beta with the same λ\lambda.

Part (iii) is an approximation to first order, not an identity. No component can anticipate a change of θb,t\theta_{b,t} that the past labels and the inputs xtx_{t} carry no information about, since by part (iv) of Proposition 6 only information that predicts θb,t\theta_{b,t} raises what a gate can promise. Part (i) explains why per-bin gates decide less than threshold gates at the same target: they ask every accepted bin to reach the target, while the promise asks it only of their mixture. Part (ii) is a Bayesian statement under a correctly specified model, not a finite-sample frequentist guarantee, and it does not survive a misspecified evolution. Part (iii) places the forgetting Beta of the loop and of the recalibration arm inside the family as its simplest member. On simulated Bernoulli streams with a level, a ramp and a seasonal path, the two give predictive means within 0.010 of each other on average with 5 labels per window and within 0.0006 with 100, for λ\lambda between 0.8 and 0.95. The proof is in Appendix A, and parts (i) and (ii) are checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib (proofs/DynamicGate.lean). The closest frequentist counterpart is conformal PID control [Angelopoulos et al., 2023], whose scorecaster forecasts the next conformal score with seasonal and exogenous models, building on adaptive conformal inference [Gibbs and Candès, 2021]. It controls the coverage of intervals rather than the accuracy among accepted decisions.

Streams with a pattern.

Two streams of 9,000 items add a known cycle to the setting of Section 10. In S1, Portuguese items are mixed with the same items after typing noise at 20%, and the share of noisy items at item tt is 12​(1−cos⁡(2​π​t/2000))\tfrac{1}{2}\big(1-\cos(2\pi t/2000)\big), so the cycle degrades the model and recurs every four windows. In S2, Portuguese and English items alternate with the same share, a cycle that, like D2, does not degrade the model. The seasonal variants are given the period, as a deployment would know a daily or weekly cycle, and the inputs xtx_{t} are two window means computed from the texts alone, the share of words absent from the Portuguese training vocabulary and the share of 30 frequent English function words. The level discount, tuned on the tuning streams of Section 10, is δ=0.80\delta=0.80. Each comparison follows the protocol of Section 4.7, paired over 30 streams per cycle and 60 per drift, with the margin of 0.02 on the share of windows below α\alpha. It is exploratory, written before the runs, and not corrected for multiplicity.

What the adapter changes.

Where the cycle or the change does not degrade the model, the dynamic variants only add cost (Table 15). On S2, D2 and the control stream, recalibration keeps the promise in every window, and against it the level model costs 0.007 to 0.010 more per item and the seasonal models about 0.07 more, all paired intervals above zero, because they escalate more without any window to repair.

Where the cycle degrades the model and its period is known, the seasonal components help the promise and pay for it in reviews. On S1 they cut the share of windows below α\alpha from 51% under recalibration to 32% (paired difference −0.19-0.19, [−0.25,−0.12][-0.25,-0.12]), and the inputs add nothing measurable (31%). The gain comes with 267 more labels per 1,000 items, which buy 16 fewer wrong actions per 1,000 and raise the cost by 0.10 ([0.09,0.11][0.09,0.11]), a trade-off. The lower-bound variant brings the windows below α\alpha to 8%, at a cost of 0.91. Learn then Test qualified again in every window does better on this stream than any dynamic variant, with 0.7% of windows below α\alpha at a cost of 0.49 and 334 labels per 1,000 items. When the cycle is fast, re-qualifying the threshold every window serves the promise better than predicting the accuracy of each bin.

Under the degrading drifts, the level model keeps the promise more often than recalibration and at a lower cost. The share of post-change windows below α\alpha falls from 57% to 28% in D1 ([−0.34,−0.25][-0.34,-0.25]) and from 38% to 23% in D3 ([−0.18,−0.12][-0.18,-0.12]), with the cost lower by 0.014 and 0.017 (both intervals below zero) and 147 and 80 more labels per 1,000 items. In D3 it costs 0.010 less than Learn then Test per window ([−0.020,−0.0005][-0.020,-0.0005], exploratory) with 82 fewer labels per 1,000 items, but its share of windows below α\alpha, 23% against 21%, is not shown to be non-inferior.

The gain comes from forgetting faster, not from the dynamic model. By part (iii) of Proposition 7, the level model with δ=0.80\delta=0.80 is, to first order, the forgetting Beta with λ=0.80\lambda=0.80, while the recalibration arm was tuned on a grid that stopped at λ=0.90\lambda=0.90, the value it chose. Recalibration with λ=0.80\lambda=0.80, run on the same streams to separate the two, matches the level model: their costs differ by at most 0.004 per item on every stream, the level model is equivalent to it on S1, S2 and the control stream, leaves 2.2 more points of post-change windows below α\alpha in D1 ([0.6,3.8][0.6,3.8]) and shows no detectable difference in D3. Against the tuned recalibration, the faster forgetting lowers the share of windows below α\alpha by 31 points in D1 and 16 in D3 at a lower cost, and costs 0.011 to 0.013 more per item on the streams that do not degrade the model. The tuning grid of the recalibration arm stopped short of the better rate.

For a caller, the reading is the following. A known cycle that degrades the model justifies seasonal components only when more reviews are affordable, and even then re-qualifying a threshold every window is the stronger option. A cycle or a change that does not degrade the model needs no dynamic component. Under an abrupt degradation, what helps the per-bin gate is to forget faster, whatever model implements it.

10.5 Numeric decisions over real time

The streams above are built from text. To see a gate on decisions about numbers, over real time and in a domain with financial series, we use the 1,428 monthly series of the M3 competition [Makridakis and Hibon, 2000]. The decision is whether the next value of a series exceeds its last one, at each of its last 36 time points, so that each time point, an origin, is a window of 1,428 decisions. The decider is exponential smoothing with additive error, damped trend and seasonality of period 12 [Hyndman et al., 2002], refitted at every origin on the last 48 observations, whose probability of a rise is the predictive probability that the next value exceeds the last. Threshold gates are calibrated once on origins 1 to 12, or on the 12 origins that precede each origin and slid by one. The per-bin gates of Section 10.4 are warmed up on origins 1 to 12, and the dynamic model gets a seasonal pair of period 12 origins. The promise is the accuracy among acted decisions in each origin, for targets of 0.60, 0.70 and 0.80. Jev and Laya decide on a sample of 150 series, 25 per category, at the last 12 origins, with the last 24 values as the state. Laya is fine-tuned in sliding blocks, on 8,000 decisions of the other series at the 24 origins before each block of six test origins, with three seeds. The analysis is exploratory and was written before the runs.

A typed decider does not read the direction of a series written as numbers (Table 16). Laya collapses onto one answer, a fall or no change in 99.7% of the decisions as released and a rise in every decision after fine-tuning, and its accuracy is that of the constant answer in both cases, 0.476 and 0.522. Jev answers a rise in 23% of the decisions, and its accuracy, 0.540 with interval [0.514,0.568][0.514,0.568], contains the 0.522 of always answering a rise. Exponential smoothing, ETS in the table, reaches 0.673 on the same decisions, and its 100 most confident decisions are right in 88% of the cases. For a decision about numbers, the decider is a model of the series, and the gate goes on top of it.

At a target of 0.60 every gate keeps the promise in every origin, because the decider is right in 67% of all decisions. At 0.70 and 0.80, threshold gates, whether calibrated once or slid over the preceding origins, fall below the target in 17% to 50% of the origins, while the per-bin gates never do (Table 17). A threshold calibrated on pooled origins promises the accuracy of their average, and the accuracy of the next origin varies around it. The per-bin gates pay in decisions, acting on 282 to 382 per 1,000 against 763 to 828 for the threshold gates at a target of 0.70, and part of their record comes from asking every accepted bin to reach the target, which by part (i) of Proposition 7 makes them conservative, so the two families are two operating points rather than one method better than the other. The seasonal pair of the dynamic model adds nothing measurable over the forgetting Beta here. The picture holds in the 145 financial series, where exponential smoothing is right in 65% of the decisions and, at a target of 0.70, the sliding Learn then Test gate falls below the target in 29% of the origins with 622 decisions per 1,000, against 4% for the per-bin gates with 266 to 294. The selective ceiling leaves room for a demanding promise: the 1,000 most confident of the 34,272 test decisions are right in 97% of the cases.

For a caller, a promise made for each period is kept only by a gate that checks each period. A threshold calibrated on a pooled past keeps the average and breaks in a third to a half of the periods at a demanding target, while tracking the accuracy of each confidence bin keeps it at the price of acting on fewer decisions.

11 When an explanation of a typed decision is useful

The deletion curves of Section 11.1 ask whether one ranking of words points to what a decision rests on. A caller who acts on an explanation needs more than a ranking. It needs to know which words carry the decision, whether they carry it alone, together or interchangeably, and how far that statement can be trusted when the decider returns probabilities rounded to two decimals, as Jev does. The problem is practical. Before acting on a decision, escalating it or auditing it, the caller wants to know whether a small change to the input could overturn it, and which words that change would touch. This section treats the explanation of one decision as a cooperative game over the words of the state and asks, for each kind of explanation, under which conditions it answers that question. Two conditions of use matter most, access to unrounded probabilities, as with open weights, and a closed API that returns two decimals. Each claim was measured against a criterion frozen before any report item was read, and the criterion decides what is reported, while its use for the caller is stated at the end of each part. Every implementation choice was recorded before the run it affects, and the changes made after a failure are stated where they occur.

11.1 Probability is not explanation

Removing the words that occlusion ranks first makes the decision fall faster than removing words at random in all four configurations measured (Figures 9 and 18). The explanation therefore carries information on average. The decision-level question is different. The Spearman correlation between the probability of a decision and the area of its deletion curve is +0.25+0.25 for the fine-tuned multilingual checkpoint and −0.38-0.38 for the same checkpoint without fine-tuning, in Portuguese, and −0.13-0.13 and +0.09+0.09 for the multilingual and English checkpoints in English: weak to moderate, and of varying sign. A smaller area means a more faithful explanation, so a negative correlation means that more confident decisions have more faithful occlusion explanations. Two Portuguese utterances illustrate it with the fine-tuned checkpoint. “qual é a diferença horária entre a califórnia e nova york” is decided as datetime_convert with probability 0.997, and the word “horária” alone accounts for 0.995 of it (area 0.05): the decision rests on one word, and changing that word changes it. “me notificar sobre os eventos no meu calendário” is decided as calendar_set with probability 0.9999, and no single word changes the decision (area 0.998): the evidence is redundant and occlusion does not reveal it. The probability does not distinguish the two situations. Jev cannot be measured this way from frozen answers, since through the API each utterance would require one request per perturbation.

11.2 The decision as a coalition game

The units of an utterance are its words when it has at most eight, and otherwise eight contiguous spans of nearly equal length, so that d≤8d\leq 8 units give 2d2^{d} coalitions. For a coalition SS, xSx_{S} keeps the units in SS and deletes the others. With jj the option decided on the full utterance and k∗k^{*} the runner-up, the value of SS is the log-odds y⁡(S)=logit⁡pj​(xS)y(S)=\operatorname{logit}p_{j}(x_{S}) or, when two options are compared, yj​k∗​(S)=log⁡pj​(xS)−log⁡pk∗​(xS)y_{jk^{*}}(S)=\log p_{j}(x_{S})-\log p_{k^{*}}(x_{S}). The game is enumerated exactly, and every attribution below is a function of it [Robnik-Sikonja and Kononenko, 2008; Zintgraf et al., 2017; Covert et al., 2020]:

mT=∑U⊆T(−1)|T|−|U|​y​(U),Fi=m{i},Wi=y⁡(N)−y⁡(N∖{i}),m_{T}=\sum_{U\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|U|}\,y(U),\qquad F_{i}=m_{\{i\}},\qquad W_{i}=y(N)-y(N\setminus\{i\}), (15)

where mTm_{T} are the Möbius terms [Fumagalli et al., 2024], FiF_{i} is the effect of a unit added to the empty state, WiW_{i} is the occlusion effect of Section 11.1 in log-odds, and EiE_{i} is the exact Shapley value [Shapley, 1953; Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Sundararajan and Najmi, 2019]. Deleting a unit is one choice of removal among several [Covert et al., 2020], so a second operator, which replaces each removed word by a training word unrelated to the options, is used as a check.

A method that ranks the units defines an order π\pi. Its deletion area is ∑k=1d[y⁡(N)−y⁡(N∖π1..k)]\sum_{k=1}^{d}[y(N)-y(N\setminus\pi_{1..k})], and the statistic uiu_{i} is the percentile of that area among all d!d! orders of the same item, with ties counted as one half. A value ui=1u_{i}=1 means that no order makes the decision fall faster. Unlike the area of Equation 8, uiu_{i} is not normalised by the initial probability and compares each item only with itself.

The four Laya cases are the multilingual and typed-decisions checkpoints in Portuguese and English, on the 1,000 report items of each language. Jev was enumerated in versions 1.13 and 1.14 on the same items, with all coalitions of an item packed in one request at a total cost of US$2.51, at the price of US$0.042 per million input tokens with output tokens free of charge, as stated by the vendor in October 2026. A stability check comes first. Asked the same question three times, Jev returns the same decision in 99.3% of the items, but only 94.7% (version 1.13 against the frozen answers) and 94.8% (1.14, between repetitions) of its probabilities stay within 0.01, below the preregistered 95%. The Jev analyses therefore use fresh answers only. Most Jev games are censored: the full utterance is returned with probability at least 0.995 in 71% to 79% of the items, depending on version and language.

What the empty state already decides.

A typed decider returns a distribution even for an empty state, and the coalition game records it as y⁡(∅)y(\varnothing). The decision on the empty state measures how much of a decision the model would take without reading the input. Against a chance level of 0.20 from the option positions, the decision on the empty state agrees with the decision on the full utterance in 21% to 23% of the items for the multilingual checkpoint, 27% to 28% for the typed-decisions checkpoint and 27% to 29% for Jev, and in 41.9% (95% interval [38.8,45.0][38.8,45.0]) for the multilingual checkpoint fine-tuned in Portuguese. A different quantity takes almost the same value: that checkpoint answers 42% of the items correctly with no input at all, against 18% for the same checkpoint before fine-tuning. Fine-tuning thus nearly doubled the share of the decision that the options alone carry. The share follows the frequency of the intents in the training data. On the empty state, the fine-tuned checkpoint picks the most frequent training intent among the five options in 65.7% of the items (95% interval [62.8,68.6][62.8,68.6], against 20% without a frequency preference), and the Spearman correlation between its empty-state probabilities and the log frequency of the intents is 0.59. Before fine-tuning the same checkpoint picks it in 14.7% of the items, with a correlation of −0.20-0.20. The pattern is consistent with fine-tuning having installed the label frequencies of the training set as a prior that the decision carries before reading any word, a reading based on one fine-tune and a correlation of 0.59. The empty state is the same in both languages, so the figures do not depend on the locale. For a caller, the empty-state probe is a one-request audit of how much of a decision is structural rather than read from the input.

Pairwise terms suffice for the game.

If the game were dominated by interactions of order three or more, no pairwise account of a decision could be faithful. The least-squares projection of yy on the constant, the units and their pairs explains a median share of 0.86 to 0.93 of the variance over the 2d2^{d} coalitions in the four Laya cases (Table 19), above the criterion of 0.6. Truncating the Möbius expansion at order two is a different and worse approximation, with negative median shares, so the order-two model is fitted, not read off the expansion. For inputs of up to eight units, an account of a decision by single words and pairs is therefore adequate. The exact game costs at most 256 passes of an open-weight decider and, with the coalitions of an item packed in one request, about US$0.0006 per decision of Jev. The exact game is also the cheaper route in model passes. It needs a median of 64 passes per decision on these items, against 514 for KernelSHAP with 256 pairs of coalitions, and the exact Shapley value then takes about 0.1 ms on one CPU thread. The Gibbs sampler of the Bayesian model of the next subsection adds 60 to 83 ms per item.

11.3 Credible intervals under rounding

The order-two model of a game is y⁡(S)=β0+∑i∈Sβi+∑i<k∈Sγi​k+εy(S)=\beta_{0}+\sum_{i\in S}\beta_{i}+\sum_{i<k\in S}\gamma_{ik}+\varepsilon, with normal priors whose scales τ1,τ2\tau_{1},\tau_{2} are chosen on calibration items by marginal likelihood. A probability rounded to two decimals only places y⁡(S)y(S) in an interval, unbounded when it reads 1.00, so the likelihood is interval-censored and the posterior is sampled by Gibbs with truncated-normal augmentation. The posterior gives 90% intervals for Wi=βi+∑kγi​kW_{i}=\beta_{i}+\sum_{k}\gamma_{ik} and Ei=βi+12​∑kγi​kE_{i}=\beta_{i}+\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{k}\gamma_{ik}. Because the exact values of Jev are unknown, the criterion is applied to Laya with its probabilities rounded as Jev’s are, and the coverage of one unit per item is scored with the ascending Beta rule. The interval should contain the exact value with a lower bound L≥0.85L\geq 0.85.

It does not (Table 19). The intervals of WiW_{i} cover 58.8% of the exact values in Portuguese and 55.4% in English, and those of EiE_{i} 63.8% and 71.8%. The sampler is correct: with the truth drawn from the prior, it covers 90.3%, and 88.3% with half of the coalitions censored at 1.00. With an exact order-two truth fitted to calibration games, coverage falls to 81%, and to 72% to 74% when the full utterance reads 1.00. The shortfall lies in what rounded data can identify. When a decision and most of its coalitions read 1.00, the data say that the log-odds exceed logit⁡0.995\operatorname{logit}0.995 and nothing about how far. In Portuguese, 84% of the items have at least one unit whose removal leaves the rounded probability at 1.00.

The two published uncertainty-aware estimators of the Shapley value do no better on the same rounded games and the same event. The unbiased KernelSHAP of Covert and Lee [2020], which covers 90.8% and 89.6% on unrounded calibration games with five and eight units, covers 59.2% and 63.2% of the exact EiE_{i}. BayesSHAP [Slack et al., 2020] covers 30.7% and 33.3% on its own probability scale and 24.2% and 22.8% in log-odds. Paired on the same items and units, the Bayesian intervals cover more often than KernelSHAP in English (71.6% against 63.2%, exact McNemar p<0.001p<0.001), no difference is detected in Portuguese (63.5% against 59.2%, p=0.051p=0.051), and they cover more often than BayesSHAP on either scale in both languages (p<10−40p<10^{-40}). Under two-decimal rounding, none of the methods tested yields a calibrated interval for the effect of a word. By the preregistered reading, the Bayesian intervals are reported as descriptive, and Jev is reported with the bounds that rounding alone identifies, Wi∈[a⁡(N)−b⁡(N∖{i}),b⁡(N)−a⁡(N∖{i})]W_{i}\in[a(N)-b(N\setminus\{i\}),\,b(N)-a(N\setminus\{i\})], where [a⁡(S),b⁡(S)][a(S),b(S)] is the log-odds interval of the rounded probability of coalition SS. These bounds are often one-sided or absent. Across the two versions and languages, 58% to 67% of the units have no finite bound, because the decision and the utterance without the unit both read 1.00, and only 19% to 25% have both bounds. They still answer part of the caller’s question. In 60% to 70% of the decisions at least one unit is certain to lower the log-odds of the decision when removed, while the unit that matters most is identified in only 17% to 21%. The version matters more for the explanation than for the decision. Versions 1.13 and 1.14 take the same decision on 98.6% of the Portuguese and 99.1% of the English items, but give disjoint identified sets for 13% and 10% of the units, so an explanation obtained through the API holds for the pinned version only. The posterior means of the order-two model, reported without a criterion as preregistered, give the same picture. The paired difference of EiE_{i} between versions has a median of −0.03-0.03 (Portuguese) and −0.07-0.07 (English) with interquartile ranges of [−0.29,0.19][-0.29,0.19] and [−0.38,0.17][-0.38,0.17] in log-odds, its sign changes for 7% of the units, and the unit with the largest effect changes in 8.6% and 9.9% of the items. For a caller of a closed API that rounds, the consequence is direct. None of these methods provides a usable uncertainty statement about the effect of a word, and the failure is not confined to censored decisions, since on the uncensored ones the intervals of WiW_{i} still cover only 60% to 68%. A caller with unrounded probabilities and inputs of up to eight units does not need such intervals, because the exact game gives the effects themselves. A second regime, which fits the same model to 256 random coalitions of unrounded games, covers held-out coalitions (92.1% and 89.4%) but not WiW_{i} (48.5% and 58.5%), and leaves the article as preregistered.

11.4 Unique, redundant and synergic evidence

The second utterance of Section 11.1, whose decision survives the removal of any single word, is a case of redundant evidence. An explanation that distinguishes such cases from evidence carried by one word, or only by two words together, would tell the caller what kind of change can overturn a decision. The protocol of Bastings et al. [2021] gives a planted truth. Five invented tokens are inserted into the Portuguese training data with forced labels: one token that decides an intent alone (unique), two interchangeable tokens for a second intent (redundant), and two tokens that decide a third intent only together (synergic). The multilingual checkpoint learns all three in three seeds, with a lower bound on accuracy between 0.968 and 0.994.

Learning a rule is not the same as encoding it in the shape the rule suggests. The Möbius signature of the planted type, for instance mA1​A2≤−12​min⁡(mA1,mA2)m_{A_{1}A_{2}}\leq-\tfrac{1}{2}\min(m_{A_{1}},m_{A_{2}}) for the redundant pair, holds in every redundant test item, but only in 35% to 38% of the unique items and 3% to 6% of the synergic ones. A unique token alone drives the probability of its intent to 1 in single precision, which leaves no room for the main effect to separate from its interactions, and in the synergic case each token alone already moves the log-odds by a median of 2.4, while the joint term is about 17. The planted truth is kept only for the redundant type.

On that type, the Bayesian model fails. Its macro F1 over the labels unique, redundant, synergic and none is 0.300, against 0.901 for the pairwise Shapley interaction index on the same rounded game, 0.889 for HEDGE [Chen et al., 2020] and 0.773 for the sign of Wi−FiW_{i}-F_{i}. The exact unrounded Möbius terms reach 0.632. A plausible reason, not tested here, is that the interval-censored posterior leaves the pairwise terms of saturated coalitions too uncertain for any credible interval to exclude zero. Under rounding, the interaction indices that average over many coalitions recover the planted redundancy, and the Bayesian decomposition does not. For the caller’s question, whether removing one word can overturn a decision, the useful tool is therefore an interaction index or HEDGE on the observed game, which works through the API as well. The planted test supports this use for redundant evidence, the case of the second utterance of Section 11.1, and not for unique or synergic evidence.

11.5 Confidence and the faithfulness of the Shapley order

Section 11.1 found the correlation between a decision’s probability and its occlusion area weak and of varying sign. The coalition game allows a sharper version of the question. A hierarchical model relates uiu_{i} of the exact Shapley order to the log-odds of the decision,

ui∼𝒩⁡(μi,si2+σ2),μi=αc⁡(i)+bc⁡(i)​logit⁡p0​i+η​di,u_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{i},\,s_{i}^{2}+\sigma^{2}),\qquad\mu_{i}=\alpha_{c(i)}+b_{c(i)}\operatorname{logit}p_{0i}+\eta\,d_{i}, (16)

with intercepts and slopes partially pooled over the intent c⁡(i)c(i) of the decision, fitted by NUTS with four chains. The non-centred parameterisation was adopted after the centred fits failed to converge (R^\hat{R} up to 1.51), and the sign of bb had already been seen when the change was made. For Jev, uiu_{i} is averaged over 100 posterior draws of the order and sis_{i} is its standard deviation, and only the uncensored items enter.

In all four Laya cases the posterior probability of a positive slope is 1.00 to two decimals (Table 19). The effect is small: bb lies between 0.004 and 0.010 per unit of log-odds, so ten units of log-odds raise uiu_{i} by 0.04 to 0.10 on a scale where its mean lies between 0.93 and 0.95, and the Spearman correlation between p0p_{0} and uiu_{i} is 0.20 to 0.25. In Jev’s uncensored stratum, of 207 to 284 items, the sign is decided in one of four cases. The model is checked on the planted checkpoint: it places the three planted intents at ranks 2, 3 and 6 of 56 by αc\alpha_{c}, within the top 10% required. For Laya, then, a more confident decision has a slightly more faithful Shapley order. The relation is too weak for the probability to select which explanations to trust. The measure here, the fidelity of the Shapley order, differs from the deletion area of Section 11.1, and the two agree only in that the relation is weak, while its direction depends on the checkpoint and on the measure. A caller who needs a faithful explanation of a decision has to measure it for that decision, at the cost given above.

11.6 Explanations across options and orders

A typed decider receives its options from the caller, and an explanation of jj against k∗k^{*} could change when the other three options change. On 200 items per language, the three options other than jj and k∗k^{*} were replaced twice by other intents, and the set of units with the largest Wij​k∗W^{jk^{*}}_{i} was compared with the original. The rate of change was then compared with that of a placebo in which the original options are only permuted. The difference DD shows approximate invariance in three of the four comparisons and a dependence in one (D=0.167D=0.167, 95% interval [0.024,0.310][0.024,0.310], Portuguese, second replacement). The evidence is thin. In about 75% of the items the replacement changes the decision or the runner-up, so the item leaves the comparison, and the remaining 42 to 52 items per comparison give wide intervals. Jev, with the largest Wij​k∗W^{jk^{*}}_{i} taken from the posterior mean of the order-two model on its rounded difference game, shows approximate invariance in all eight comparisons of the two versions and languages, with 68% to 76% of the items excluded for the same reason. That exclusion rate is itself the finding that matters for use. A contrastive explanation holds for the option set it was computed on, and when the caller changes the options it has to be recomputed rather than reused.

On the same items, six orders were scored by uiu_{i} under both removal operators and for both deletion and insertion. The rankings of the methods agree across operators, with Kendall’s τ\tau between 0.6 and 1.0. Paired over items under deletion, the exact Shapley order deletes faster than the occlusion order WiW_{i} of Section 11.1 in all six cases of Laya and Jev, by 0.05 to 0.23 in percentile, and faster than KernelSHAP in all six, by 0.007 to 0.013. Against BayesSHAP the difference is detected in three cases, against the first-entry order FiF_{i} in five, and against HEDGE in none, so the exact Shapley value and HEDGE share the lead. Occlusion, the cheapest explanation, is among the two least faithful by its own criterion of deletion. The mean percentile of the Shapley order under deletion is 0.92 in Portuguese and 0.93 in English, so the best order is close to, but not at, the fastest possible. On Jev’s rounded games the same ranking appears in all four cases, with Kendall’s τ\tau between 0.6 and 1.0, and occlusion falls further behind, with a mean percentile of 0.71 to 0.75 against 0.94 to 0.96 for the Shapley order. Rounding leaves the occlusion effect at exactly zero for most units, so its order is decided by the tie-break. When a single ranking of words is wanted for a short input, the exact Shapley order or HEDGE is the one to use, and occlusion, though the cheapest, is the one to avoid.

11.7 An additive head

A head built so that the contribution of each word is exact loses 28.7 points of accuracy in Portuguese and 31.8 in English, and the head that results is additive in positions rather than in words. Exactness by construction is therefore not a useful route to explanations here, and the measurement is reported in full in Appendix C.

12 A validation protocol

Two kinds of validation are needed: of each statement made about a decider, and of each decision it takes. For statements, we tag every claim with its source: documentation (what the vendor states, on the access date), code (what the program does, at a pinned commit), measured (what happened on our data, reproducible with the released script and seed), and not published (nothing can be asserted). The tags matter in practice. Between 2026-09-29 and 2026-10-20 the vendor documentation changed from a text-only input to experimental image input and a new model version, 1.14, and a statement made without a date became false without anyone changing it. A vendor statement can also be tested, as the one about probability 1.0 was.

For decisions, we group the operational controls into seven, a grouping that the same talk also uses [IBM Technology, 2026], and turn each into a measurement with the instruments of Section 4 (Table 20). None of them requires access to the model’s internals, so all apply equally to the open and the closed decider. Only the measurement of explanation fidelity does.

For comparisons between methods, the definitions of Section 4.7 turn a reading of means into a statement that another team can check. Four practices carry most of the weight. The margin is fixed before the data, from the smallest difference that matters or from a stated tolerance, and written down with its reason. Non-inferiority and equivalence are claimed only by their tests, and an interval that contains zero is reported as no difference detected. Resources are measured alongside the outcome, so that a method that keeps the promise at a lower cost is credited and a method that saves one resource by spending another is reported as a trade-off. And the uncertainty of every difference includes the sampling of the items, not only the Monte Carlo error of the procedure, since in the gate of Section 6.3 the Monte Carlo error alone would show a detectable coverage gain in 21 of the 24 combinations, against 4 once the item part is included.

13 What a caller can do

The sections above end with what their measurements mean for whoever deploys a typed decider. Table 21 gathers those readings in one place, each with the measurement behind it.

14 Limitations

Most measurements use one dataset, MASSIVE, with five options per question. The language front extends them to 52 locales without fine-tuning beyond Portuguese, and the battery to four further domains with two to six options, but each of those domains is one dataset. Only exact duplicates of test utterances were removed from the fine-tuning set. Near duplicates may remain and inflate the accuracy of the fine-tuned checkpoints. The deletion area is normalised by the initial probability and capped at one, so when that probability is close to one, as for the fine-tuned checkpoint, its range is restricted and the correlation with the probability is partly mechanical and attenuated. The fine-tuned checkpoints were trained in Portuguese only. Jev was measured mostly in version 1.13, with version 1.14 only in the explanation front, and its rounding to two decimals limits every analysis that needs its probabilities near one. Laya probabilities are stored with five decimals and clipped at 10−610^{-6} before temperature scaling. Occlusion measures one kind of explanation and produces inputs unlike the training data. The coalition games of Section 11 delete words and inherit that limitation, which the replacement operator only partly addresses. Their gates were evaluated on Laya rounded to two decimals as a stand-in for Jev, which assumes that rounding, not the model, drives the failure of coverage. The planted truth holds for the redundant type only. The noise of Section 7 is synthetic, drawn from a fixed set of operators, and the traffic of a real deployment may hold other kinds, such as abbreviations, mixed languages and voice transcription errors. The cost ratios 10:1 and 100:1 are illustrative scenarios. The gate is evaluated on random splits of one fixed sample, which makes calibration and report items exchangeable. Under drift or with correlated items, such as consecutive video frames, neither the Beta rule nor Learn then Test keeps its promise without further assumptions.

15 Conclusion

A typed decider’s “0.97” licenses a statement about groups: among many answers given with that confidence, about 97% are right, provided the decider is calibrated on the data at hand. It does not certify a single answer and it does not explain the decision. The measurements here make each of these limits concrete, and the gate turns them into an engineering choice: separate calibration from decision, choose the threshold from the cost of errors, and state the promise as a conditional accuracy that the threshold rule must sustain on new data. A point estimate breaks such a promise in 147 of the 190 exchangeable evaluations measured here. A lower bound keeps it. Learn then Test does so with a guarantee, in all 190 exchangeable evaluations here. The ascending Beta rule, which differs from it only in the prior and the order of the scan, decides more items on average than Learn then Test in 128 of them and fewer in none, a gain the item-level uncertainty of the static front does not confirm after correction for multiplicity, at a violation rate that stays near the nominal level without a guarantee, demonstrably above 5% in one evaluation, at 5.5%. It is the better trade when more automatic decisions matter more than a formal guarantee, and it gains most with the weakest decider. Every counting rule depends on the order of the confidences rather than on their calibration, which a Bayes threshold does not escape. The same reading applies to explanations. For short inputs the exact coalition game of a decision is affordable, also through Jev’s API, and it says which words carry the decision and whether they carry it interchangeably. Rounding to two decimals takes away the uncertainty statement. Through the API a caller can certify that some word matters in most decisions but rarely which matters most, and an explanation holds only for the pinned version and for the options it was computed on. Under drift the exchangeability behind every rule here fails, and the measurements again say when a method helps rather than whether it wins. The Bayesian loop avoids needless retraining where the stream is stable or its change harmless, at a cost equivalent to recalibration alone and lower than that of periodic retraining and DDM. Under a drift that degrades the model it reacts late and does not improve on periodic retraining, and the arms that keep the promise most often re-qualify the threshold in every window and pay for it in reviews. The labels that every loop consumes can also come from the people who receive the decisions, by marking each answer right, partly right or wrong, which turns the audit sample into online calibration data and is the setting we leave for future work. The ablation credits the loop’s trigger and shows that its re-qualification step, the ascending Beta scan on hard recent labels, is where the promise breaks. On real news streams, where the change from year to year is mostly mild, the loop has the lowest mean cost in nine of ten transitions, five of which do not pass the preregistered check of degradation, and the preregistered summary over the five that do detects no difference.

A promise also does not travel by itself. Calibrated in English, Jev keeps a promise of 95% in 8 of 51 locales, a fine-tuned Laya needs from 250 to 8,000 labels to match Jev depending on the domain, and on the direction of a numeric series neither decider does better than a constant answer, while exponential smoothing is right in 67% of the decisions. The rule for a caller follows from all of this: calibrate on data that looks like the traffic, choose the threshold with a lower bound, check the promise again when the traffic changes, and audit the decisions the gate takes alone.

Data and code availability

The reference package is deposited on Zenodo [Brom, 2026], doi:10.5281/zenodo.23676316: the parallel items in the 52 locales, Jev’s decisions with the probability of the decided option, Laya’s probabilities for every option, the coalition games, the drift runs and a datasheet. Jev’s probabilities for the options not decided are not distributed, since the vendor’s customer agreement forbids using its output to train a model that imitates it. The code, including promise_check and its test, and the derived measurements and figures are available at https://github.com/pcbrom/typed-deciders-audit and in the same deposit. The fine-tuning recipe and the lesson material are at https://github.com/pcbrom/laya-jev.

Use of AI-assisted tools

AI-assisted tools were used for code development and English language editing. Experimental design, analysis and interpretation are the author’s.

Proof of Proposition 3.

A rule that decides from CC accepts on a set S⊆[0,1]S\subseteq[0,1]. Its expected cost is 𝔼[𝟏[C∈S]Ce(1−A)+𝟏[C∉S]Cr]=𝔼[𝟏[C∈S]Ce(1−ℙ(A=1∣C))+𝟏[C∉S]Cr]\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{1}[C\in S]\,C_{e}\,(1-A)+\mathbf{1}[C\notin S]\,C_{r}\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{1}[C\in S]\,C_{e}\,(1-\mathbb{P}(A=1\mid C))+\mathbf{1}[C\notin S]\,C_{r}\big]. Under top-label calibration ℙ⁡(A=1∣C=c)=c\mathbb{P}(A=1\mid C=c)=c, so the integrand at C=cC=c is Ce​(1−c)C_{e}(1-c) if c∈Sc\in S and CrC_{r} otherwise. The pointwise minimum is attained by including cc in SS exactly when Ce​(1−c)<CrC_{e}(1-c)<C_{r}, that is c>1−Cr/Cec>1-C_{r}/C_{e}. Ties may be resolved either way. Pointwise minimisation of the integrand minimises the expectation. □\square

The Beta posterior of eq. 10.

With θ∼Uniform⁡(0,1)=Beta⁡(1,1)\theta\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)=\mathrm{Beta}(1,1) and cc successes in nn exchangeable Bernoulli(θ\theta) trials, the posterior density is proportional to θc​(1−θ)n−c\theta^{c}(1-\theta)^{n-c}, which is Beta⁡(c+1,n−c+1)\mathrm{Beta}(c+1,n-c+1). Its predictive mean (c+1)/(n+2)(c+1)/(n+2) is Laplace’s rule of succession, used per confidence bin in the gating rule under drift.

Appendix B What each route costs

This appendix holds the cost comparison summarised in Section 6: the measured costs of each route, the break-even between a local fine-tune and a priced API, and the effect of the processor’s instruction set on local inference.

What each route costs.

Table 5 puts the measured costs side by side. Jev needs no labels and no training, and a decision costs 384 input tokens at the price stated by the vendor, US$0.016 per 1,000 decisions. Its latency was not measured. Laya runs locally in about 12 ms per item on a CPU. Fine-tuned on subsets of the training partition with three seeds and compared item by item with Jev’s frozen answers, it is non-inferior to Jev, with the 2-point margin of Section 4.7, from 4,000 labels on (paired difference 0.0 points, 95% interval [−1.5,1.5][-1.5,1.5]), and more accurate with the full 11,274 (1.5 points, [0.1,2.9][0.1,2.9]). At 3,500 labels the lower bound is −2.1-2.1, just outside the margin. Training on 4,000 labels takes 17 seconds on one GPU. The fixed cost of the local route is the labelling, which was not measured and depends on the domain. With cℓc_{\ell} the cost of a label, LL the number of labels and pp Jev’s price per decision, the local model pays for its labels after

N∗=L​cℓpN^{*}=\frac{L\,c_{\ell}}{p} (17)

decisions. N∗N^{*} is a lower bound, since local inference is not free either. At an illustrative cℓc_{\ell} of US$0.05 and L=4,000L=4{,}000, N∗N^{*} is 12 million decisions, and at US$0.50 it is 124 million. Unless the volume reaches tens of millions of decisions, the price per call therefore barely enters the choice between the two models. What decides it is whether the state may leave the machine, whether each decision must be auditable, and whether the accuracy required is beyond what the closed model reaches without labels, as it is for the fine-tuned checkpoint here. Rewritten as L​cℓ≤N​pL\,c_{\ell}\leq N\,p, the condition is a product, and Figure 10 draws its boundary for any price of a label, any number of labels and any API price.

The processor sets part of the local cost.

The 12 ms of Table 5 use bfloat16 autocast on a CPU with AVX-512 BF16 instructions. On that processor (AMD Ryzen 9 9900X3D, six threads, batches of eight sorted by length), the released multilingual checkpoint takes 30.0 ms per item in Portuguese and 29.7 in English in float32, 14.1 and 13.8 ms in bfloat16 autocast and 11.0 and 10.8 ms with the encoder quantised to int8 on the fly. Against float32 on the same items, bfloat16 is equivalent by two one-sided tests with the 2-point margin (Portuguese −0.3-0.3 points, 95% interval [−0.7,0.0][-0.7,0.0], English +0.1+0.1, [−0.2,0.5][-0.2,0.5]) and keeps the decision in 99.7% and 99.6% of the items, a clean gain of 2.1 times in speed. Dynamic int8 is 2.7 times faster but loses 4.2 points in Portuguese ([−6.9,−1.5][-6.9,-1.5]) and 2.9 in English ([−5.2,−0.7][-5.2,-0.7]), changes 25.6% and 17.2% of the decisions and is not non-inferior, so its speed is bought with accuracy. On a processor with the bfloat16 instructions the faster precision is therefore free, and the cheaper integer one is a trade-off that has to be measured on the task before it is used.

Appendix C An additive head

The additive head summarised in Section 11 is reported here in full.

An explanation that is exact by construction requires a model whose decision is a sum over words [Agarwal et al., 2020]. Attention layers do not learn additive models on their own [Leemann et al., 2024], so the additive form has to be imposed. In the additive head, each state token tt contributes et,j=LN⁡(ht)⊤​U​V⊤​LN⁡(m~j)e_{t,j}=\operatorname{LN}(h_{t})^{\top}UV^{\top}\operatorname{LN}(\tilde{m}_{j}) to the logit of option jj, with U,VU,V of rank 64 and m~j\tilde{m}_{j} the representation of option jj with an empty state. The logit is a bias plus the sum of these contributions, so the state enters only through the sum. The head was fine-tuned with the recipe and seeds of the original head.

Over three seeds, the additive head reaches an accuracy between 0.614 and 0.749 in Portuguese and between 0.589 and 0.713 in English, against 0.960 to 0.972 for the original head trained the same way. The paired loss is 28.7 points in Portuguese (95% interval [−30.8,−26.6][-30.8,-26.6]) and 31.8 in English ([−34.1,−29.7][-34.1,-29.7]). With seed 0 its training accuracy is 0.692, so the loss is underfitting rather than overfitting. Its calibration error after temperature scaling is also higher, with 95% intervals of the paired difference in ECE of [0.021,0.051][0.021,0.051] and [0.027,0.055][0.027,0.055], and the ascending Beta gate at a target of 95% decides 260 to 379 items per 1,000, against 998 to 999 for the original head, while breaking its promise in 8% to 11% of the partitions, against none. The word scores do not explain even the additive model itself. On the 770 Portuguese report items with at least five units, their mean Spearman correlation with the exact Shapley value of yj​k∗y_{jk^{*}} in the same model is 0.024, below the 99th percentile of a within-item permutation null (0.035), and a median 69% of the summed evidence falls outside the word tokens, on special tokens and the final separator. On the original head, occlusion reaches 0.567 against its own exact Shapley value and SLALOM, the additive surrogate of Leemann et al. [2024], 0.840. By the criterion, the head is additive in positions, not a self-explanation by word. The preregistered fallback adds to the logit a residual rjr_{j} from the original head, penalised by λ​meanj​rj2\lambda\,\mathrm{mean}_{j}r_{j}^{2}, and reports the additive share, the median over items of the variance across options carried by the additive sum relative to the sum and the residual together. With seed 0 the penalty works as a dial. At λ=0.01\lambda=0.01 the residual carries the decision (share 0.0003, accuracy 0.970 in Portuguese and 0.967 in English), at λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 the share is 0.62 with an accuracy of 0.967 and 0.961, and at λ=1\lambda=1 it is 0.996. Because λ=1\lambda=1 was singled out after seeing seed 0, its two further seeds are exploratory. Over the three seeds it keeps an additive share of 0.996 to 0.998 at a paired loss of 3.7 points in Portuguese ([−4.7,−2.7][-4.7,-2.7]) and 3.8 in English ([−4.9,−2.8][-4.9,-2.8]), with an ECE of 0.06 to 0.09 against 0.01 to 0.02 for the original head. Its word scores now track its own exact Shapley value above the permutation null (mean Spearman 0.226 against 0.035), but far below occlusion and SLALOM on the original head, and 58% of the evidence still falls outside the words. By the criterion it is a measured cost, not a competitive head, and it is additive in positions rather than by word. For this problem neither head is a useful route to exact explanations. The pure additive head costs about 30 points of accuracy and does not explain itself, the penalised residual costs about 4 points and worse calibration and still does not explain itself by word, and for short inputs the exact game of the original head gives exact attributions without any loss.

Appendix D Repairing the re-qualification of the loop

The second ablation of the drift loop, summarised in Section 10, is reported here in full.

Repairing the re-qualification.

A second ablation, designed after the first and therefore exploratory, separates three causes on the same streams, one change at a time. Re-qualifying only on the held-out labels that decided the promotion, which the new model was not trained on, repairs D1: the share of post-change windows below the promise falls by 9.2 points ([−15.8,−2.6][-15.8,-2.6]) and the cost by 0.016. It does not help in D3. The fixed-sequence scan in place of the ascending one repairs D3, lowering that share by 21.7 points ([−29.8,−13.5][-29.8,-13.5]) at the price of 124 more labels per 1,000 items, and weighting each audited item by the inverse of the audit rate, so that the calibration sample represents the stream, lowers it by 17.9 points ([−25.2,−10.6][-25.2,-10.6]) with a lower cost. Neither changes D1 detectably. The causes therefore differ by drift. Under new scenarios the threshold fails because it is chosen on items the model has just been trained on, and under a label change it fails because the ascending scan and an unrepresentative sample pick a threshold the stream does not support, the failure that Proposition 4 describes. The three changes together keep the gain in D1 (−9.5-9.5 points) and lose it in D3 (−0.4-0.4, [−6.1,5.3][-6.1,5.3]). A plausible reason, not tested here, is that the held-out sample is small, the weights shrink its effective size further, and no threshold then qualifies, so the loop keeps the old one. The pair without weights, fixed-sequence scan on held-out labels, was not run.

Real streams.

Ten year-to-year transitions of News Category headlines, five orders each, were run with all nine arms. The manipulation check keeps five transitions, those starting in 2013, 2015, 2016, 2018 and 2019, whose frozen model loses 2.6 to 36.6 points of accuracy across the year boundary. In the other five the frozen model loses less than 2 points or improves, and they are reported but left out of the summary, as preregistered. Over the five kept transitions, treated as clusters, the loop is cheaper than the periodic arm by 0.27 per item on average, with a 95% interval of [−0.58,0.04][-0.58,0.04] that contains zero, so the preregistered summary detects no difference. Transition by transition the direction is the same in all ten, kept or not, and the loop has the lowest mean cost of the nine arms in nine of them. The exception is the transition with the largest drop, from 2013 to 2014, where Learn then Test per window is cheapest (0.86 against 0.95 for the loop and 1.64 for the periodic arm). On the share of windows below the promise the transitions disagree (interval [−0.90,0.35][-0.90,0.35]). As supporting evidence, the real streams agree with the synthetic reading. Where the change is mild, as in most year transitions of news headlines, the loop is the cheapest arm, and where it is large and abrupt, re-qualifying the threshold wins.

Appendix E Gate at all targets, split-half evaluation

The split-half evaluation draws 1,000 random partitions of the 2,000 items into a calibration half and a report half (seed 20261021), fits the temperature and the threshold on the first and measures accuracy among accepted items on the second. Its rates include report-side noise and serve to attribute effects in Section 6.4. The promise itself is judged against the plug-in population in Table 7.

Appendix F Reference table by language

Table 23 gives, for each locale of MASSIVE 1.1, the accuracy of the three deciders on the 1,000 parallel report items and the violation rate of the promise of 95% by the ascending Beta rule, calibrated on the en-US calibration items or on the calibration items of the locale (Laya only, since Jev answered the report items alone in the new locales). The pt-PT and en-US answers of Jev are those of the noise run of Section 7. Intervals, non-inferiority to en-US, ECE, decisions and the other rules are in the released file analise_multilingue.json, and the same table as CSV in tabela_linguas.csv.

Appendix G Report cards of the battery

Table 24 gives one block per domain of Section 9, with the same layout for all, MASSIVE pt-PT first as the reference measured with the same code. Each promise cell reads violation rate over decisions per 1,000, against the plug-in population with 2,000 draws, so a cell such as 0.00/0 is a promise kept by deciding nothing. The released and fine-tuned Laya are calibrated by temperature on each draw, and Jev is used as returned. The label curves are in Figure 8, and every value with its interval is in the released file analise_bateria.json.
